entries.title: Boy, 17, shot in North Lawndale
entries.summary: <p>A 17-year-old boy was injured in a shooting Sunday night in North Lawndale. </p><p>The teen boy was standing outside around 8:35 p.m. in the 1300 block of South Independence Boulevard when someone opened fire, Chicago police said. </p><p>He was struck in the arm and lower back, police said. He self-transported to Mount Sinai Hospital, where he was in good condition. </p><p>Police said the shooter fled the scene. No arrests were made. </p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: 2 critically wounded in Roseland shooting
entries.summary: <p>A man and woman were shot while standing outside Sunday afternoon in the Roseland neighborhood on the Far South Side. </p><p>They were in the 11000 block of South Normal Avenue when they were approached by an armed male who shot at them around 4:30 p.m, Chicago police said. </p><p>The man, 31, was shot in the wrist, abdomen and clavicle. He transported himself to Roseland Hospital, where he was in critical condition, police said. The woman, 40, was wounded in the arm and was taken in critical condition to Christ Medical Center in Oak Lawn.</p><p>No arrests were made. </p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: D'Avilla, Lod score in Fire's victory against visiting Timbers
entries.summary: <p>Dje D'Avilla had a goal and an assist in the first 14 minutes and the Fire spoiled the debut of Portland Timbers coach Martí Cifuentes with a 2-1 victory on Sunday night at Soldier Field.</p><p>D’Avilla picked up his second assist on a goal by Robin Lod in the 9th minute and then scored for the first time this season five minutes later to give Chicago a 2-0 lead.</p><p>Defender Andrew Gutman also had an assist — his fourth — on Lod's fourth netter. Maren Haile-Selassie notched his seventh assist on D'Avilla's goal — one off his career high.</p><p>Defender Finn Surman used his head in the 85th minute to score his first career goal in 51 appearances and cut it 2-1. Defender Brandon Bye earned his third assist this season and Ariel Lassiter, a second-half substitute, was credited with his fourth.</p><p>Chris Brady totaled one save for Chicago (10-6-2).</p><p>James Pantemis stopped two shots for Portland (7-9-3), which made it's first trip to the Windy City in eight years. Neither keeper had a save in the first half.</p><p>The Fire moved into third place in the Eastern Conference with the victory.</p><p>Cifuentes is the Timbers' fifth head coach.</p><p><b>Up next</b></p><p>Timbers: Host San Diego FC on Wednesday.</p><p>Fire: At Orlando City on Wednesday.</p>
entries.author: AP

entries.title: Five dead in mass shooting in East St. Louis
entries.summary: <p>EAST ST. LOUIS, Ill. — Five people were killed in a “targeted mass shooting” against a family in southwestern Illinois, police said.</p><p>Two more people were wounded, and two teenagers, ages 15 and 16, were in custody, police said.</p><p>Most of the shootings occurred Sunday at three locations in East St. Louis, including a park. East St. Louis, population 17,500, is across the Mississippi River from St. Louis. It had 15 homicides in 2025, down from 34 in 2020, records show.</p><p>“It’s terrible. It’s evil. But it will not keep this city down,” Illinois State Police Director Brendan Kelly told reporters Sunday, referring to the shootings. “The progress we have made will not be lost.”</p><p>Troopers stopped a vehicle and arrested two teens suspected in the shootings, Kelly said.</p><p>A motive remained under investigation, he said. The victims who died were ages 74, 49, 25, 24 and 21. Kelly did not detail the relationship between the victims but said at least one suspect was connected to the family.</p><p>Marcus May told the St. Louis Post-Dispatch that he lost stepchildren, his mother and a sister — “my whole family in one fell swoop.”</p><p>A decision about criminal charges could come by Tuesday, St. Clair County State’s Attorney James Gomric said.</p><p>“This feels like something that would happen on ‘The First 48,’ not right across from you,” said Keveon Johnson, referring to the true-crime TV series. He lives in a public housing development where one of the shootings occurred.</p><p>City Council member Courtney Hoffman said it was not a random act of violence.</p><p>“This is not a mass shooting where you have to worry about going to the grocery store and someone opening fire,” Hoffman told KTVI-TV.</p>
entries.author: AP

entries.title: Cubs stagger into series vs. White Sox after losing Dansby Swanson and seeing Edward Cabrera get rocked
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="_blank" >Cubs</a> entered their weekend series against the Cardinals as one of the hottest teams in the majors. They had won nine of their last 12 games and were beginning to creep up on the National League Central-leading Brewers.</p><p>Now they’re entering a three-game set Monday against the White Sox in a much worse place.</p><p>The Cubs lost 11-4 on Sunday to drop the last two games of the series and fall five games behind the Brewers. Shortstop Dansby Swanson will get an MRI exam and is headed to the injured list after hurting his left oblique on a swing in the third inning, and right-hander Edward Cabrera returned from the IL to give up seven runs in 3 2/3 innings.</p><p>No, that’s not the way to step into <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/16/white-sox-cubs-crosstown-rivalry-wrigley-field-chicago" target="_blank" >the biggest Cubs-Sox series at Wrigley Field</a> and the teams’ most high-stakes matchup since the 1906 World Series. The Sox have a 5½-game lead in the American League Central, just swept the Tigers in Detroit, beat the Cubs twice in May and have powerful bats that can punish pitching mistakes — something the Cardinals did by scoring a combined 19 runs Saturday and Sunday.</p><p>Swanson won’t be around to help cover for any pitching issues. And that will be an adjustment because he has played in 119 of the Cubs’ 125 games this season and in at least 147 in each of his three full seasons since joining them as a free agent.</p><p>‘‘I just want to play and do everything I can to win,’’ Swanson said. ‘‘In the meantime, people call me ‘Coach’ for a reason, so I can find some fun ways to be useful.’’</p><p>Swanson will watch Nico Hoerner shift to shortstop and rookie Pedro Ramirez get the bulk of the playing time at second base. Though Hoerner is a strong shortstop, the Cubs know their defense — a huge strength — will be somewhat diminished without Swanson for at least 10 days and possibly much longer if the MRI reveals bad news.</p><p>‘‘We can cover it,’’ Hoerner said. ‘‘We have great athletes on our team and good depth, but there’s no replacing Dansby. Anytime you have moving parts in the middle of the field, it is a challenge.’’</p><p>Getting the most from Cabrera also has been a challenge, and the Cubs didn’t receive much from him Sunday.</p><p>Cabrera had been out since June 24 with a strained left hamstring but wasn’t exactly giving the Cubs quality starts before that. He had a 5.10 ERA in 72⅓ innings and was falling well short of justifying the Cubs’ decision to send the Marlins a package that included outfielder Owen Caissie to acquire him.</p><p>Nothing Cabrera did Sunday indicated he should be counted on for the rest of the season, and the Cubs might feel the same way about him as a starter. Manager Craig Counsell said the team will discuss whether Cabrera will take his next turn in the rotation.</p><p>Cabrera got only 10 swings-and-misses, and Counsell said the separation in velocity between his changeup and fastball wasn’t enough to make a difference.</p><p>‘‘It didn’t go well,’’ Counsell said.</p><p>Cabrera said he has a blister on his right middle finger, which was bandaged when he talked with the media, but Counsell didn’t mention that during his postgame briefing.</p><p>Early in the game, Cabrera said he felt a ‘‘sensation’’ and tried to pitch through it. But he felt it the most in the fourth, which is when he was removed and told Counsell and the staff.</p><p>If the blister isn’t an issue, Cabrera is optimistic he’ll remain in the rotation.</p><p>‘‘One hundred percent [confident],’’ he said through a translator.</p><p>The Cubs won’t be 100% when they see the Sox.</p>
entries.author: Brian Sandalow

entries.title: Sky hold on for 82-80 road victory against the Storm
entries.summary: <p>SEATTLE — Kamilla Cardoso had 22 points and 12 rebounds, Natasha Cloud scored 20 points and the Sky ended a six-game losing streak on the road with an 82-80 victory against the Seattle Storm on Sunday at Climate Pledge Arena.</p><p>Seattle (7-30) trailed 53-37 with 5:49 left in the third quarter, but Dominique Malonga answered with a basket and two free throws and Jade Melbourne and rookie Awa Fam sank back-to-back three-pointers to cap a 15-4 run as the Storm closed to 60-55 heading to the fourth.</p><p>Seattle pulled within a point, but Courtney Vandersloot sank the second of two free throws for the Sky (13-22) with 10 seconds left and Melbourne missed a tying layup at the buzzer. Vandersloot finished with 15 points, five rebounds, five assists and four steals.</p><p>‘‘I’m just proud of the team for how they fought,’’ Sky coach Tyler Marsh said. ‘‘I thought we got great contributions across the board.’’</p><p>Seattle made the first basket, but Cardoso scored six in an 11-0 run and Chicago never trailed again.</p><p>Malonga had 19 points and 13 rebounds for Seattle, which snapped an 11-game losing streak with a 97-88 win over the visiting Sky on Monday. Ezi Magbegor had 17 points and Fam scored 14 off the bench.</p><p>The Sky won despite shooting just 36% (27-for-75), including just 26% (6-for-23) from three-point range.</p><p>The Sky are technically still alive for a playoff berth but trail eighth-place Dallas by seven games with nine games left to play.</p>

entries.title: We’re on the hunt for Barack Obama’s tan suit. Help us find it.
entries.summary: <p>The opening of the museum in the Obama Presidential Center this summer sparked an unintended consequence: a new wave of interest in former President Barack Obama’s famous tan suit.</p><p>The Obama tan suit that launched one of Washington’s <a class="Link" href="https://archive.nytimes.com/runway.blogs.nytimes.com/2014/08/28/obama-wore-a-tan-suit-and-spoke-about-world-crises/" target="_blank" ><u>most absurd controversies</u></a> when he wore it to an Aug. 28, 2014, press conference.</p><p>The tan suit that inspired a hilarious <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=crNcV0k0aMQ" target="_blank" ><u>press conference skit</u></a> starring Obama and Larry David on the August finale of their HBO sketch series.</p><p>The suit that is not in the museum.</p><p>The legendary suit reporters were told Obama gave away when he was cleaning out a closet.</p><p>I’m on assignment to find Obama’s tan suit.</p><p>I don’t know when Obama gave it away or to whom.</p><p>This is more than hunting for a needle in a haystack. I don’t even know where the haystack is.</p><p>I wasn’t sure at first how to proceed. It’s not like the suit was taxpayer-funded traceable public property or an official gift that had to be transferred to the National Archives and Records Administration upon leaving office.</p><p>So I just jumped in. I made an initial list of 68 people to call to get the ball rolling. On my punch list: I needed to know who made Obama’s tan suit — the origin story.</p><p>And I found, with the help of a pal, the not widely known genesis of the tan suit. It was made by Martin Greenfield, who sewed his first stitches when he was a prisoner at Auschwitz, repairing the torn shirt of an SS soldier. After the young teen survived the Auschwitz and Buchenwald Nazi concentration camps, Greenfield eventually became a famous tailor in Brooklyn, New York.</p><p>When I first tell people I’m on the hunt for Obama’s tan suit, I can hear their eyeballs rolling. When I tell them a Holocaust survivor who came to the U.S. made the suit — well, something clicks and they want to know more about my project.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Photos of Martin Greenfield with Barack Obama and Bill Clinton hang on the wall at Martin Greenfield Clothiers in Brooklyn, New York. In the top photo, Greenfield (left) and his sons Tod and Jay (right) pose with Obama.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Zubaer Khan/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Greenfield died in 2024. His sons run the company now. I recently talked to one son, Jay, who went to the White House to measure Obama for suits. I’ll have lots more to pass along from my interview with Jay in another column.</p><p>But first, let me explain my tan suit project. The journey will unfold in print and the digital world. We’ll have videos. Maybe some events. And I’ll be reaching out to you to figure out what the uproar over the suit means in 2026 — and why some folks thought it should be in the museum.</p><p>The suit triggered a political firestorm when Obama wore it to a press conference where he talked about crises in Ukraine and the Middle East. Critics said he looked un-presidential. Supporters said the criticisms were racially based.</p><p>The Obama tan suit controversy touched on the raw fault lines surrounding race in this nation. Other presidents — Ronald Reagan, for example — wore tan suits with impunity. But not the nation’s first Black president.</p><p>I don’t accept that the Obama tan suit is lost forever, because I haven’t tried hard enough yet to find it.</p><p>What we know is the tan suit is having a moment.</p><p>Let me tell you what we saw during the June 19 Obama Presidential Center dedication. Marty Nesbitt, the chair of the Obama Foundation, came to the stage dressed in a re-creation of the famous outfit: tan suit, white shirt, copycat striped tie. Guests like former late-night stalwarts Stephen Colbert, David Letterman and others also <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/fashion/2026/06/18/revenge-of-the-tan-suit-at-the-obama-presidential-center-ceremony" target="_blank" ><u>wore tan suits</u></a> to the ceremony.</p><div data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Nesbitt’s getup was a surprise — and very intentional. He had a statement to make.</p><p>When Obama saw Nesbitt, the former president got up from his seat, embraced his friend and said, “I love that tan suit.”</p><p>Nesbitt said it was “inspired by a very good friend of mine who made tan suits famous. And I don’t know about the rest of you all, but I thought he looked pretty good wearing his, so I decided to wear one myself. … [This] is my way of just showing a whole lot of love.”</p><p>Rewind to June 3. I’m at a press preview briefing at the Obama Presidential Center.</p><p>Obama Foundation CEO Valerie Jarrett and Michael Strautmanis, the Obama Foundation chief corporate affairs officer, are among the briefers. Strautmanis is asked what he wished was in the museum that’s not there.</p><p>“Tan suit,” he said.</p><p>Jarrett delivered the bombshell.</p><p>“The reason we don’t have the tan suit is President Obama gave it away when he was cleaning out his closet,” she said. “But we thought about a replica, but that would not be authentic, and so, we do not have the tan suit.”</p><p>Colbert, former host of “The Late Show,” is one of the people who expected the tan suit to be in the museum.</p><p>Last May, in one of his last episodes, Colbert interviewed Obama in the museum. The comedian demanded to know if “the tan suit is here.”</p><p>Looking over a photo of the infamous 2014 press conference, Obama told Colbert, “I look great.” But he didn’t mention he gave it away.</p><p>In the HBO show, “Life, Larry and the Pursuit of Unhappiness,” the Obama and David spoof creates a fictional comic backstory about why Obama wore that suit to the press conference. The show was produced by Barack and Michelle Obama through Higher Ground, their company.</p><p>It was taped in December in an Obama-era Oval Office recreated on a Los Angeles soundstage. In the skit, Obama wears a tan suit with a jacket that’s a spot-on ringer of the original. However, it was a replica, made by costume designer Christina Mongini.</p><p>So, the hunt continues.</p><p>I understand why this assignment ended up in my lap. Until last year, I was the longtime Washington Bureau Chief at the Chicago Sun-Times. A highlight of my career was covering Barack Obama from the Senate to the White House, to his post-presidency and the development of the Obama Presidential Center.</p><p>I was not shocked about the tan suit in 2014 because I had seen Obama out of his dark-suit uniform. I was with him on Aug. 23, 2006, when the then-Illinois senator wore a beige suit while visiting the Illinois Africa Office for Trade and Investment in Johannesburg. (That office no longer exists.) I was surprised when I saw Obama wearing a light-color suit but never thought of writing about it.</p><p>The night before my interview with Jay Greenfield, I was in a panic because I never got a copy of <a class="Link" href="https://www.regnery.com/9781684515080/measure-of-a-man/" target="_blank" ><u>Martin Greenfield’s memoir</u></a>, “Measure of a Man: From Auschwitz Survivor to Presidents’ Tailor.” I was kicking myself for being unprepared.</p><p>I ran over to the Highland Park Public Library, and to my relief, they had the book. When I was checking it out, I explained why I wanted it, because I want to enlist everyone in my cause. I see that as part of this project — telling everyone what I am doing to see if one thing can lead to another.</p><p>I chatted with library membership services staffer Dara Bass and told her about the connection between the book, Obama’s tan suit and my tan suit project.</p><p>The next day, Bass sent me a note.</p><p>“Your storyline is interesting,” she wrote, because “it highlights the origin story of the bespoke garment and a human behind it. Moreover, your angle is unique because it sort of shifts the focus from the person who donned the clothing (in the spotlight) onto the person whose hard-earned skill and expertise led him to create it (behind the scenes).”</p><p>I don’t know how this quest for Obama’s tan suit ends. But I do know how it begins.</p><p><b>Contact us</b>: Please join us on this journey by sending tips, story ideas or suggestions on who to interview. Email: tansuit@suntimes.com.</p>

entries.title: Three sought in slaying of man in Chicago Lawn
entries.summary: <p>Police are looking for three attackers who were fighting with a 29-year-old man when one of them drew a gun and fatally shot him Sunday night in the Chicago Lawn on the Southwest Side.</p><p>The man, 29, was standing in the 6100 block of South Campbell Avenue around 10 p.m. with three attackers when an argument turned physical and one of the three opened fire and shot him about the body, police said. </p><p>He was taken to the Advocate Christ Medical Center in Oak Lawn where he died, police said. </p><p>The three fled and have not been arrested. </p><p>Area 1 detectives were investigating. </p>

entries.title: Families of dead found improperly stored never got chance to grieve, honor loved ones
entries.summary: <p>Fifty-six bodies were found at <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/06/decomposing-bodies-found-funeral-home-south-chicago-chapel-95th-street" >South Chicago Chapel</a>, and a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago/2026/08/07/owners-of-far-south-side-funeral-home-have-history-of-mishandling-human-remains" >Chicago Heights crematory operated by the same owners</a> shut down last year for the same offense.</p><p>Mayor Brandon Johnson called the reports about what took place at South Chicago Chapel as a violation of trust. It was. But there is an older word for what was taken.</p><p>A funeral is not a service loved ones purchase. It is a rite — one of the oldest things our species still does. It is a ceremony during which the living formally hand over their dead to the earth or spirit world. Denied it, grief does not settle into memory. It simply goes on.</p><p>I have spent my life conducting concerts. A concert cannot be attended on your behalf. It exists only while it is happening; when it stops, nothing survives of it but the memory of the people who were there. A funeral is the same. Being told your mother was cremated is not the same as having stood there while she was.</p><p>Consider the family from the Chicago Heights crematory who waited two years for an urn, kept it and only later learned the ashes inside were not their mother's. They had grieved in good faith over a stranger. No fine covers that.</p><p>What was taken was not money. It was the hour in which sorrow is permitted to become memory.</p><p>Yet that hour belongs to no funeral home, and it has not expired. After World War I, Europe filled with cenotaphs — empty tombs raised for men who were never found — and the words spoken there were not spoken in vain. A rite requires the living, gathered and someone willing to say the words. The body cannot always be had. The gathering can.</p><p><i>David Woodard, Tampere, Finland</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-240000" name="module-240000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Save — don’t trash — school supplies</h3><p>As Chicago families gear up for another school year, a devastating cycle is quietly repeating in school hallways across our city, especially at the former Acero charter schools now being run by Chicago Public Schools: tons of perfectly usable school supplies are being <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/08/04/dumpsters-full-of-books-showed-up-outside-former-acero-schools-parents-and-teachers-worked-to-salvage-them" >tossed</a> directly into dumpsters.</p><p>At the <a class="Link" href="http://www.creativechirx.org/" target="_blank" >Creative Chicago Reuse Exchange</a>, we see this waste firsthand. When classrooms are cleared out, pristine notebooks, binders, unopened packs of markers and art supplies are routinely discarded. This is not just an environmental failure, it is a community tragedy.</p><p>Right now, many teachers in underfunded Chicago classrooms spend hundreds of dollars of their own money on basic learning tools. Meanwhile, standard surplus supplies are headed to landfills.</p><p>We must shift our mindset from disposal to redistribution. Our organization, along with local creative reuse networks like Reduce Waste Chicago, stands ready to accept these materials and get them into the hands of educators and students who need them most. Our semi-annual <a class="Link" href="https://www.creativechirx.org/post/2026-teachers-back2school-supply-giveaway" target="_blank" >Teacher Back2School Supply Giveaway </a>event, scheduled for Aug. 21-22, would be the perfect destination for all this unused surplus.</p><p>We urge CPS administrators, principals and teachers to partner with Creative Chicago Reuse Exchange's local reuse organizations before the next clean out day. Let’s teach our children a vital lesson in sustainability and community care by keeping these valuable tools out of the trash and in the classroom.</p><p><i>Barbara Koenen, founder and executive director, Creative Chicago Reuse Exchange</i></p><h3>ICE and its gruesome gloves </h3><p>Imagine you step out of your home, bright and early at 6 a.m. What do you see? Peace, love and kindness? No, not anymore. Instead, you may soon see U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents with gloves that can hurt and maybe even kill. These <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/ice-electric-shock-gloves-85ff746d3e0ee5f39e7a9a3f1f576252" target="_blank" >gloves deliver electric shocks</a> that, according to one lawsuit, contributed to a man's death in Kentucky.</p><p>You may soon hear screams of pain and distress. This could happen to you or a loved one. It is not funny, a meme or a joke. This is our lives. Only we can fight, protest and abolish ICE. The people of our city are pleading with you to help. We need to stop ICE. Stop Donald Trump. Don't let what happened in Minneapolis and Chicago happen again. Don't stand for this. I'm 12 years old, and we know that ICE is brutal. Let's stop this madness.</p><p><i>Benten Ortiz</i>, <i>John B. Murphy Elementary School student</i>, <i>Belmont Cragin</i></p><h3>West Side youth gears up for triathlon</h3><p>While many students spent their summer break on their electronic devices or playing video games, some West Side youth spent the last few months training for the <a class="Link" href="https://supertri.com/chicago/" target="_blank" >Supertri Chicago</a>, the triathlon scheduled take place Aug. 22. Thanks to the multi-functional community facility <a class="Link" href="https://breakthrough.org/" target="_blank" >BreakThrough FamilyPlex</a> and the nonprofit <a class="Link" href="https://www.livegritsoars.org/" target="_blank" >Live Grit SOARS</a>, students were able to seize this opportunity.</p><p>Our team has athletes between the ages of 7 and 22. Some of our youth just started to learn how to swim this summer. This is not surprising, as many people of color never had access to learn such skills. According to The<a class="Link" href="https://www.usaswimming.org/" target="_blank" ><u> </u>USA Swimming Organization</a>, 64% of African American and 45% of Hispanic/Latino have little to no swimming ability.</p><p>There's limited access to pools in West Side schools. In addition, most of our youth don't have the chance to experience Chicago's free public beaches and lakefront the way tmany others from more affluent neighborhoods do. But we will not let that stop us!</p><p>Our participants have been training at least three days a week since summer started. Many community-based nonprofit organizations and dedicated volunteers have also been helping by ensuring the children have proper supplies, including swimwear and running gear, as well as a bike to borrow for the race.</p><p>Our goal is to inspire future athletes and encourage others from our community to be a part of something positive. Our youth deserve to be showcased for their perseverance through adversity. We are defying the odds.</p><p><i>Karonda Locust, Garfield Park</i><br></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: No-Kids Wedding Reception Plan Upsets Grandparents
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My youngest son is getting married this spring, and they have decided they want a child-free wedding reception. We have three grandchildren, ages 3 to 7. The wedding is where my son and his fiancee live, so we are all traveling. They have asked all three kids to be in the wedding party as flower girls and the ring bearer, but afterward there is a sit-down meal, reception and dance to which the kids are not invited. The parents are expected to find or bring babysitters.</p><p>Our grandchildren are extremely important to my husband and me, and we are devastated they have been excluded. We see them as part of the immediate family and have asked that they be included, but the bride and groom have declined our requests. They have also banned babies of any age, nursing or not, yet their dog is part of the wedding party.</p><p>I was at the bride's wedding shower this past weekend, along with my two other daughters-in-law, and I tried to feel enthusiastic about their upcoming wedding, but it is difficult. I have shed a few tears over this and have become resentful of both of them. Do you have any advice? — <i>WEDDING WOES IN CANADA</i></p><p><b>DEAR WEDDING WOES:</b> I'm sorry the wedding reception isn't going to be the joyous family moment you were hoping for. If you and your husband were to renew your vows, I'm sure the festivities would be much different. However, this day is for the bride and groom. They are planning the celebration they want, and that includes a reception they've deemed inappropriate for kids. Show your love and respect for them by leaving your expectations — and your grandchildren — at the hotel.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> An acquaintance of mine has posted pictures of his newly built mansion, from breaking ground to digging the huge pool to the house itself. I admit I'm jealous. But isn't this rude of him? All our friends are middle to upper class. I find it terribly insensitive. Am I wrong? — <i>FLIPPING MAD IN TEXAS</i></p><p><b>DEAR FLIPPING MAD:</b> I'm sorry your ego is bruised from looking at the photos your friend posted of creating his new home, but what he did isn't rude. Perhaps if you start counting the blessings you have in your own life, you can combat the green-eyed monster you have been feeding. I wish you luck because there is nothing constructive about envy.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> Should I tell my two older grandchildren that my husband and I are divorcing? Although the divorce is in its early stages, our home is expected to be sold a year and a half from now. My daughter and grandchildren reside in that home. I'd like to know if this would be too early to let them know. Please give me your opinion. — <i>MAKING A CHANGE IN FLORIDA</i></p><p><b>DEAR MAKING A CHANGE:</b> Your daughter should be told (if she doesn't already know) because she will need time to find another home for herself and her children. When to share the news of the divorce with her children should be her decision. A year and a half is plenty of time for everyone to prepare for the changes that are coming. I hope that the divorce will be amicable.</p>

entries.title: Bears take 'ownership' of Ben Johnson's offense, which should lead to faster start when season arrives
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> coach <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/09/01/the-bears-and-their-fans-needed-a-truth-teller-they-got-one-in-new-coach-ben-johnson" target="_blank" >Ben Johnson</a> is happy — his word, believe it or not — with his offense, and that’s quite a leap from how he felt a year ago.</p><p>While it never would be quite correct to describe him as calm, he has been relatively low-key this training camp because things are running so much more smoothly than they did in his first one. There has been no need to light a fire under his players, as he did repeatedly last season.</p><p>‘‘I feel really good about where those guys are at,’’ Johnson said, noting that the first-string offense went through 60 simulated plays before sitting out the preseason opener Saturday against the Browns. ‘‘I’m happy with what the offense looks like right now. Yet we’re only halfway through this thing, and we have a long way to go.’’</p><p>Always something to strive for, of course.</p><p>Last August, Johnson shredded the offensive players on the practice field and at the podium for sloppiness, slowness and a general inability to get on his level. At one point, quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/08/31/why-do-so-many-people-hate-bears-qb-caleb-williams-he-answers-exactly-that-question" target="_blank" >Caleb Williams</a> said to himself, ‘‘This dude doesn’t seem like he likes me.’’</p><p>It wasn’t surprising at all that he felt that way. Johnson was on him at every turn, especially about delay-of-game penalties and other pre-snap errors, and took his frustrations public multiple times:</p><p>† After the Bears’ 10th practice of camp, a debacle at Soldier Field, Johnson railed on the offense for being ‘‘sloppier than we were hoping we would be at this point’’ and warned, ‘‘If it continues like that, we’re not going to win many games.’’</p><p>† A few weeks later, he was beside himself and talked openly about downsizing his playbook, questioned Williams’ vision in the pocket and graded the overall group as ‘‘not good enough.’’</p><p>† In mid-September, well beyond when he thought the problems would be in the past, he unleashed his harshest criticism yet: ‘‘Our practice habits are yet to reflect a championship-caliber team’’ because of poor effort, fundamentals and other ‘‘little things that you learn in youth-league football.’’</p><p>There hasn’t been any of that this time around. Johnson has been fiery and energetic on the practice field, but there haven’t been any blow-ups. There have been ups and downs, certainly, but he has liked what he has seen overall.</p><p>‘‘My concerns last year were a lot with the pre-snap [issues]; we don’t have those procedure issues to that degree anymore,’’ Johnson said. ‘‘Provided we can keep those to a minimum, that’s where we’ll continue to get better.’’</p><p>He views the next two weeks as an ideal test of that progress. Is it real? He thinks he’ll find out in the joint practice Thursday with the Bengals in Cincinnati and in another one a week later with the Titans. Whether the starters play in the ensuing preseason games against those teams might hinge on how sharp those practices are.</p><p>Experience has played a big role in the Bears having a more peaceful camp this season. Of their top 13 offensive players (their starters plus an extra tight end and running back), 11 were on the team last season. The other two are wide receiver Kalif Raymond, who was with Johnson for four seasons with the Lions, and center Garrett Bradbury, an eight-year veteran who started for the Patriots in the Super Bowl last season.</p><p>Another memorable moment in Johnson’s first camp came when he was asked to list the players he trusted to know the plays and could name only four.</p><p>When he was reminded of that Saturday, he said he couldn’t even put a number on it. And when a rookie such as Zavion Thomas looks lost, Johnson tells him to watch fellow wide receivers Rome Odunze or Raymond.</p><p>That means it’s no longer just Johnson’s offense, as it was when the Bears were learning it last summer. Now it’s fully wired into the players, moving the team closer to the full version of what Johnson envisions.</p><p>‘‘You see a lot more glimpses of what we expect it to be,’’ offensive coordinator Press Taylor said. ‘‘Everybody knows what the standard is, what it looks like, what our pre-snap operation looks like.</p><p>‘‘They feel what it’s like to come out of the huddle with clarity, conviction on what we’re doing. . . . There’s a lot of ownership in that, which is really what you’re trying to get. When the players own the pre-snap process, it’s going to take off.’’</p><p>Theoretically, it should take off in Week 1 against the Panthers. That would be a sharp contrast from last season, when preseason miscues lasted well into the regular season.</p><p>If the Bears want to repeat as NFC North champions, establish themselves as true contenders and chase the single-season scoring record, as Johnson has said, they need to start hot. Based on how they look now, there shouldn’t be any warming up required.</p>
entries.author: Jason Lieser

entries.title: Trump's anti-diversity crusade borrows from Chicago’s past
entries.summary: <p>I spent my childhood on 74th Street and South Shore Drive, watching how Chicago negotiates the boundaries of who belongs. Long before I analyzed race and public policy for a living, I was a Hyde Park Academy graduate in the South Side legislative district Barack Obama once represented. I learned early that “merit” is not neutral when the people in power define the measure, set the threshold and decide whose qualifications are presumed credible.</p><p>That lesson has felt familiar all summer.</p><p>In June, Chicago Public Schools CEO and Supt. Macquline King <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/06/10/what-to-know-as-cps-ceo-macquline-king-prepares-to-testify-before-congress-under-subpoena" >testified before a Republican-led House committee</a> in Washington, D.C., after being subpoenaed alongside superintendents from San Francisco and Virginia. At a hearing titled “Breaking Trust,” lawmakers portrayed CPS policies involving transgender students and its Black Student Success initiative as attacks on parental rights and violations of civil rights law.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-cf0000" name="module-cf0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>That spectacle was not an isolated incident. It was part of a broader federal campaign against diversity, equity and inclusion that has only accelerated. That same month, Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul joined a coalition of attorneys general <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/06/11/attorney-general-illinois-19-other-states-sue-trump-federal-contracts-changes-dei" target="_blank" >challenging the Trump administration’s DEI restrictions on federal contractors</a>.</p><p>Trump's <a class="Link" href="https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/03/31/2026-06286/addressing-dei-discrimination-by-federal-contractors" target="_blank" >Executive Order 14398</a> directs federal agencies to add contract terms restricting DEI-related practices and places existing contractors at risk of losing federal work if they will not accept them. The July 24 deadline for contractors to accept new terms has passed; litigation over the requirement is pending.</p><p>This is not a minor policy adjustment. It puts research universities, public agencies and other federal contractors under pressure to audit programs designed to broaden access and participation, often while their work depends on federal research, defense or transportation funding.</p><p>The rhetoric driving this campaign relies on a seductive story: Diversity initiatives are inherently discriminatory, trading competence for quotas and eroding a supposedly pure, objective standard of "merit."</p><p>Chicagoans should recognize that script. We have heard versions of it in our own public institutions for decades.</p><p>Consider the Chicago Fire Department’s 1995 entrance exam, <a class="Link" href="https://www.scotusblog.com/2010/02/when-is-a-test-used-for-purposes-of-title-viis-statute-of-limitations" target="_blank" >litigated all the way to the U.S. Supreme Court</a>. The city labeled applicants who scored 89 or above “well qualified” and hired almost exclusively from that group for six years, even though the passing score was 65, and the city’s own expert warned the 89-point cutoff was arbitrary. Roughly 6,000 Black applicants who had passed were never called. The city did not dispute the cutoff disproportionately excluded Black candidates. It defended the practice as neutral and job-related.</p><p>That is the crucial distinction. Standards are not illegitimate simply because they produce unequal outcomes. But neither are standards automatically legitimate because they are described as neutral. Who designed the test? Why was a passing score of 65 deemed inadequate? What evidence justified a threshold of 89?</p><p>Those questions are not an assault on merit. They are what serious institutions ask when merit is invoked to preserve an exclusionary status quo.</p><p>When national leaders now suggest that opening doors to qualified women and people of color makes an institution less capable or less safe, they are not inventing a new philosophy. They are reading from an old Chicago playbook.</p><h3>Fictitious problem</h3><p>Blaming diversity is also a political dodge. It directs public anger toward an imagined cause while actual problems remain unfunded and unresolved. After an American Airlines jet and a U.S. Army helicopter collided over the Potomac River last year, President Donald Trump <a class="Link" href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/watch-live-trump-holds-news-briefing-on-deadly-plane-collision-over-washington-dc" target="_blank" >blamed DEI </a>before investigators had completed their work. But the <a class="Link" href="https://www.ntsb.gov/news/press-releases/Pages/NR20260127.aspx" target="_blank" ><u>National Transportation Safety Board’s investigation</u></a> identified systemic failures in airspace design, safety oversight and risk management — not diversity initiatives — as central to the catastrophe.</p><p>In Chicago, the same misdirection is visible in institutions people depend on every day. The Federal Aviation Administration has <a class="Link" href="https://www.nbcchicago.com/news/local/ohare-flight-limits-to-remain-in-place-through-october-2027/3960151/" target="_blank" ><u>capped O’Hare at 2,708 daily operations</u></a>, more than 300 fewer flights than airlines had scheduled, because of operational constraints.</p><p>Chicago Public Schools, meanwhile, confronts a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-school-board/2026/07/30/chicago-school-board-approves-budget-that-reverses-layoffs-but-counts-on-shaky-state-funds" target="_blank" ><u>roughly $732 million budget gap</u></a>, and King has warned that without viable financing, the district could struggle to make payroll in September. Those are not diversity problems. They are governance, staffing, infrastructure and public investment problems.</p><p>Defending student initiatives or baseline workplace equity does not undermine institutions. What undermines them is a political reflex that fights imaginary diversity demons rather than funding the staff, infrastructure and classrooms required to keep the public safe and educated.</p><p>When leaders weaponize “merit” to dismantle equity tools, they create deeper public cynicism, especially among Black and Latino Chicagoans who have ample historical reason to question institutions charged with managing their risk.</p><p>When politicians turn DEI into a catch-all culprit for complex failures, Chicagoans should look past the spectacle and ask: What are they hoping we will not notice while we argue about the wrong thing?</p><p><i>Donathan L. Brown, Ph.D., is an associate professor at Northeastern University, a former U.S. Fulbright professor, and the author of five books on civil rights and voting rights. A native of the South Side, he graduated from Hyde Park Academy.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-120000" name="module-120000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Darren Bailey accepts campaign money from sex offender who's now pastor, attends service at his church
entries.summary: <p>Rockford resident Victor D. Barr was convicted of aggravated criminal sexual abuse in the early 2000s for having sex with a girl who attended the public high school where he taught math.</p><p>He was required to register as a sex offender, with his name, photo and address displayed on a publicly accessible State Police database for the rest of his life.</p><p>Barr’s name is now surfacing on a different list — of campaign contributors to Darren Bailey, the Republican candidate for Illinois governor.</p><p>Barr and his household made two contributions this year to the Bailey for Illinois campaign account, one for $700 in a donation dated in April and another for $400 in a donation dated in June, according to records maintained by the Illinois State Board of Elections.</p><p>A spokesman for Bailey says of Barr: "We did not know his background ... we’re going to find a charity and donate it ... we’re committed to making it right."</p><p>Also in June, Bailey attended a service at the Rockford Faith Center, a nondenominational Christian church where, since his conviction, Barr has become one of the pastors under Apostle Marla Lyon Eash, according to online accounts and interviews.</p><p>“This past Sunday at Faith Center was powerful for many reasons, but one moment before the message truly stood out,” read Faith Center’s Facebook post. “Pastor Marla had the opportunity to pray over Darren Bailey and his wife — not because he came to campaign, but because he came to worship.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a Barr and his household to Darren Bailey’s political fund.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Illinois State Board of Elections</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Eash says Bailey visited the Faith Center during that campaign, too.</p><p>There’s no rule barring sex offenders from giving money to political causes, but sensitive to the optics, many campaigns would likely refuse their contributions if they knew of a donor's history.</p><p>Reached at his home in recent days, Barr, 69, indicated he has no connection to Bailey but is a “philosophical supporter, that’s what I would say.”</p><p>Barr described himself as “a believer in Jesus Christ” and said Bailey, an evangelical Christian, has “Christian values.”</p><p>Although the Faith Center has a youth ministry, Eash says Barr has nothing to do with it and is “a wonderful man, he’s a blessing to our church.”</p><p>“He’s not a sex offender, that might have been his past life,” she said, adding he’s been “truly transformed.”</p><p>“If I don’t believe in redemption, then I shouldn’t be a pastor.”</p><p>Barr taught at Rockford’s East High School and was once nominated for a Golden Apple Award for “excellence in teaching,” according to published accounts. His victim was a 17-year-old female student who he repeatedly had sexual relations with, including at the school, according to court records.</p><p>Barr was in a “position of trust” over the victim and abused her for “the purpose of sexual gratification,” court records say.</p><p>He pleaded guilty in 2003. His current home is roughly a mile from East High School.</p>

applied for the opportunity, but only nine were selected for the showcase to vie for the coveted spot on 2026’s bill, featuring such headliners as Twenty One Pilots, Tool and Pierce the Veil. The local band contest is a part of Riot Fest’s “Beyond the Fest,” initiative, which launched in 2023 to help ease tensions with its neighbors over use of Douglass Park, a key green space in the community.</p><p>Among the talent were some previous community band winners — 2024’s VII (Seven) and 2023’s NewClear Fusion. Also in the mix were local acts Rose of Demise, Mother of Fortune, Large Mouth, Through N Through, William Baranda and his band, Fantasma Negra and LP Trixie.</p><p>Large Mouth ended up taking first place and securing a spot at Riot Fest. The teen punk rock band is made up of three brothers from Little Village — 16-year-old Jorgie Santopoalo, 15-year-old Jeremy Santopoalo and Oliver Santopoalo, their 11-year-old drummer. Friends from the neighborhood, 18-year-old Diangelo Esquivel, 16- year-olds Jeremy Abarca and Oliver Mendoza round out their six-piece ensemble.</p><p>The Community Talent showcase originally had one spot up for grabs, but in a surprise, Riot Fest Executive Director George Herrera announced at the showcase that runner-up Rose of Demise, a metal core band from the South Side, will also get to entries.title: 'Broadview 6' judge has to decide whether to hold prosecutors accountable after exposing misconduct
entries.summary: <p>Before<b> </b>voting<b> </b>to give April Perry<b> </b>a lifetime job<b> </b>as a federal judge<b> </b>in 2024, a senator<b> </b>asked<b> </b>the longtime prosecutor<b> </b>to reflect<b> </b>on one of her most significant cases — and what it taught her.</p><p>Perry<b> </b>chose the case against Jon<b> </b>Burge, the late Chicago<b> </b>police<b> </b>commander<b> </b>tied to torture claims who was ultimately<b> </b>convicted<b> </b>of perjury. Perry<b> </b>helped put Burge<b> </b>in prison<b> </b>in 2011, and she said she learned about<b> </b>the damage<b> </b>one corrupt law enforcement officer<b> </b>could do.</p><p>However, she said she also found the reverse to be true.</p><p>“When the government appropriately polices its own misconduct, punishing those who do not display the integrity that is demanded of them, it enhances community trust and respect for the police, and our community is safer,” Perry wrote to U.S. Sen. Amy<b> </b>Klobuchar.</p><p>It could be a pivotal lesson as Perry, now in her second year as a judge, decides what to do about alleged<b> </b>prosecutorial<b> </b>misconduct<b> </b>in the tainted case against the group of Operation Midway Blitz protesters <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/27/broadview-six-boutros-chicago" target="_blank" >known as the “Broadview Six.”</a></p><p>There are tremendous differences between the Burge and “Broadview Six” scandals. But trust in law enforcement lies at the heart of each of them. And the revelations in the “Broadview Six” case created an <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/23/broadview-six-boutros-mecklenburg-loretto-hospital" target="_blank" >instant credibility crisis</a> for Chicago U.S. Attorney<b> </b>Andrew Boutros’ office.</p><p>A veteran prosecutor from Boutros' office is accused of mishandling the case before a grand jury. Defense attorneys say a cover-up ensued<b> </b>to hide what happened from the judge. Now, Perry is weighing whether to hand down sanctions<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/06/17/broadview-6-want-special-counsel-to-probe-boutros-office-trumps-justice-department-for-criminal-contempt" target="_blank" >or name a special counsel</a><b> </b>to<b> </b>investigate<b> </b>Boutros<b> </b>and others<b> </b>for contempt.</p><p>Boutros<b> </b>argued<b> </b>earlier this month<b> </b>that he’s worked to prevent such misconduct from happening again, and he insisted a judge’s contempt power should only<b> </b>“be exercised with appropriate discretion.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div moment for a 47-year-old<b> </b>judge<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/donald-trump/2025/10/09/federal-judge-set-to-hear-arguments-in-high-stakes-national-guard-hearing" target="_blank" >who once blocked</a><b> </b>President Donald Trump’s attempt<b> </b>to deploy<b> </b>National Guard troops<b> </b>in Illinois and who was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/6/28/23777146/biden-intends-to-nominate-first-woman-april-perry-to-top-federal-prosecutor-spot-in-chicago" target="_blank" >tapped<b> </b>in 2023</a><b> </b>to be Chicago’s top federal prosecutor — only to be <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2024/03/10/april-perry-us-attorney-john-lausch-jd-vance-confirmation-senate" target="_blank" >denied the job</a><b> </b>by future Vice President JD Vance.</p><p>How Perry will rule now is anyone’s guess. Before the “Broadview Six” case collapsed, she sided against defense attorneys on multiple occasions. She<b> </b>even<b> </b>scolded<b> </b>one defendant's lawyers<b> </b>for pushing the very issue that led to the misconduct revelations.</p><p>But she had unmistakably harsh words for the feds May 21, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/21/broadview-ice-protest-grand-jury-transcript-kat-abughazaleh-trump" target="_blank" >the day the case fell apart</a>. Three other judges threatened hearings, and one of them actually forced Boutros into her courtroom.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/10/hearing-in-loretto-hospital-case-could-address-claims-of-prosecutors-misconduct-if-feds-dont-drop-it" target="_blank" >first threat</a> came from U.S. District Judge Sharon<b> </b>Johnson<b> </b>Coleman, an Obama appointee. She presides over a case<b> </b>tied to Loretto Hospital<b> </b>that was also handled by Mecklenburg, the former lead “Broadview Six” prosecutor.</p><p>Boutros’ office <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/11/broadview-six-grand-jury-misconduct-federal-prosecutors-drop-charges-loretto-hospital-covid-fraud" target="_blank" >avoided a hearing</a><b> </b>in Coleman’s courtroom<b> </b>by permanently dropping<b> </b>criminal charges against two defendants.</p><p>Then, a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/18/boutros-holleb-hotaling-atf-country-club-hills" target="_blank" >separate scandal</a> erupted<b> </b>over the attempted robbery<b> </b>of undercover federal officers in Country Club Hills. U.S. Magistrate Judge Keri<b> </b>Holleb<b> </b>Hotaling<b> </b>threatened<b> </b>to hold a sanctions<b> </b>hearing<b> </b>when <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/19/shooting-fbi-atf-hotaling-boutros-country-club-hills" target="_blank" >video surfaced</a> that appeared to contradict<b> </b>an FBI agent’s<b> </b>sworn affidavit.</p><p>Boutros’ office argued<b> </b>the judge<b> </b>didn’t have<b> </b>the authority<b> </b>to hold<b> </b>such a hearing. Holleb<b> </b>Hotaling<b> </b>wound up agreeing<b> </b>to<b> </b>a<b> </b>“brief”<b> </b>delay<b> </b>and has yet to reschedule.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-2d0000" name="image-2d0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8af0760/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5147x2889+0+271/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F6a%2Fc3%2Fc379d48f4ce29cd0b1de396847ed%2Fboutros-patel-blanche-dc-news-conference-07-01-26.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e150751/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5147x2889+0+271/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F6a%2Fc3%2Fc379d48f4ce29cd0b1de396847ed%2Fboutros-patel-blanche-dc-news-conference-07-01-26.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/fcef860/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5147x2889+0+271/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F6a%2Fc3%2Fc379d48f4ce29cd0b1de396847ed%2Fboutros-patel-blanche-dc-news-conference-07-01-26.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="WASHINGTON, DC - JULY 01: Acting U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche speaks during a news conference at the Robert F. Kennedy Department of Justice building on July 01, 2026 in Washington, DC. The DOJ held the news conference to discuss recent developments in the department's investigation of the Tren De Aragua gang. Blanche was joined by U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of Illinois Andrew Boutros (L) and Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) Director Kash Patel (R). (Photo by Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images) ORG XMIT: 776523909" srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/fcef860/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5147x2889+0+271/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F6a%2Fc3%2Fc379d48f4ce29cd0b1de396847ed%2Fboutros-patel-blanche-dc-news-conference-07-01-26.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/4eb8f5e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5147x2889+0+271/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F6a%2Fc3%2Fc379d48f4ce29cd0b1de396847ed%2Fboutros-patel-blanche-dc-news-conference-07-01-26.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/fcef860/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5147x2889+0+271/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F6a%2Fc3%2Fc379d48f4ce29cd0b1de396847ed%2Fboutros-patel-blanche-dc-news-conference-07-01-26.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Then-Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche speaks to reporters in Washington about an investigation into the Tren de Aragua gang. Blanche was joined by Chicago U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros, left, and FBI Director Kash Patel, right.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anna Moneymaker/Getty</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Finally, U.S. Magistrate Judge Laura<b> </b>McNally<b> </b>ordered<b> </b>Boutros<b> </b>into her courtroom<b> </b>July 9<b> </b>after he discussed<b> </b>details<b> </b>of a sealed case<b> </b>involving<b> </b>the<b> </b>Tren de Aragua<b> </b>gang<b> </b>at a press conference with then-Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche<b> </b>and<b> </b>FBI Director<b> </b>Kash Patel.</p><p>McNally found<b> </b>her order sealing the case<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/07/09/judge-finds-chicagos-embattled-u-s-attorney-violated-secrecy-order-in-tren-de-aragua-case" target="_blank" >had been violated</a>. But beyond forcing Boutros to explain himself in court, the judge ordered no sanction.</p><p>Observers wondered if McNally would go further. But harsh sanctions could trigger appeals, Wood noted. And there aren’t many tools available to judges to enforce their orders, she added.</p><p>Judges can impose monetary sanctions, report lawyers to disciplinary bodies and hold people in contempt. Wood said those “are all meaningful sanctions, but it’s not a long list.”</p><p>“I think the judges are trying to keep the process honest,” Wood said. “But at the same time, not use the most dramatic power until the need arises.</p><p>“They want to save it for the really important moments.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/27/broadview-six-boutros-chicago" >What to know about the ‘Broadview Six’ scandal rocking Chicago’s federal courthouse</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/05/boutros-broadview-six-perry" >Boutros acknowledges ‘mistakes’ in ‘Broadview 6' case but says sanctions, special counsel aren’t needed</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2024/03/10/april-perry-us-attorney-john-lausch-jd-vance-confirmation-senate" >Is time running out for April Perry to become Chicago’s first female U.S. attorney?</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/04/07/chicago-crime-justice-department-doj-boutros-trump-midway-blitz-corruption" >After rocky first year, Chicago’s top federal prosecutor says he isn’t taking orders from Washington</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Jesse White Tumbling Team ready for second chance on ‘America’s Got Talent’ as troupe rolls into live rounds
entries.summary: <p>Although many Fourth of July weekend fireworks in Chicago may have been rained out, some shone oh so brightly from as far away as California.</p><p>While it wasn’t pyrotechnics and lasers, it was dazzling nonetheless, as Chicago’s <a class="Link" href="https://jessewhitetumblingteam.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Jesse White Tumbling Team</u></a> did the city proud with their explosive audition on the new season of “America’s Got Talent.”</p><p>Their <a class="Link" href="https://youtu.be/Qd1JQqcwYAI?si=AByCESRow_gjEKam" target="_blank" ><u>televised July 7 performance</u></a> at the Pasadena Civic Auditorium garnered four enthusiastic “yeses” from show judges — Simon Cowell, Howie Mandel, Mel B and Sofia Vergara — and a thunderous standing ovation from the audience; all of it good enough to send the troupe into the reality competition series’ live rounds, which kick off on Tuesday night. Viewer votes will determine which acts move on in the competition. The ultimate prize: $1 million and a chance to headline a Las Vegas show.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/Qd1JQqcwYAI?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="92-Year-Old Jesse White And His Tumbling Team SHOCK The Judges! | Auditions | AGT"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Their winning form follows that of another Chicago organization, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/movies-and-tv/2025/09/24/chicago-leo-catholic-high-school-choir-americas-got-talent" target="_blank" ><u>Leo High School Choir,</u></a> which made it to the final five last year on “AGT,” finishing in fourth place overall.</p><p>The tumblers’ current run on the show follows a 2008 “AGT” initial audition that did not fare so well, as they failed to advance in the competitive rounds. Nearly 20 years later, the show came calling, said Emmanuel McGhee Sr.</p><p>McGhee is a 26-year organization veteran who worked his way up through the organization’s ranks to his current role as head coach/choreographer/manager. He also works full time in the Illinois Secretary of State’s Office.</p><p>“The [show] reached out to us maybe about a year ago … asking if we wanted to audition again. And, of course, we said yes,” said McGhee.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-d60000" name="image-d60000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/af94823/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe2%2F82%2F1363e6f04f41b2136008e20e491d%2Fjessewhitetumblers-260818-09.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/1edab6d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe2%2F82%2F1363e6f04f41b2136008e20e491d%2Fjessewhitetumblers-260818-09.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/1656d38/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe2%2F82%2F1363e6f04f41b2136008e20e491d%2Fjessewhitetumblers-260818-09.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Jessie White Tumblers Head Coach Emmanuel McGhee Sr. at the Jesse White Community Center, 412 W. Chicago Ave. in River North, Wednesday, Aug. 12, 2026." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/1656d38/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe2%2F82%2F1363e6f04f41b2136008e20e491d%2Fjessewhitetumblers-260818-09.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d6a4515/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe2%2F82%2F1363e6f04f41b2136008e20e491d%2Fjessewhitetumblers-260818-09.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/1656d38/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe2%2F82%2F1363e6f04f41b2136008e20e491d%2Fjessewhitetumblers-260818-09.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Emmanuel McGhee Sr. is a 26-year veteran of the Jesse White Tumblers who worked his way up through the organization’s ranks to his current role as head coach/choreographer/manager. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Nineteen tumblers are in the competition, culled from the 11 units that comprise the overall organization.</p><p>The hardest part, McGhee said, was keeping everything on the QT from family, friends and even other tumblers from last October until a week before the audition aired. The organization’s regular practices and busy schedule (more than 1,500 shows annually) served as the perfect veil for the big secret.</p><p>For the audition, McGhee choreographed a two-minute routine instead of their usual 15-minute show. Tumblers “flew in” from two directions, which is something they never do, he said. They also sped up the timing of their moves overall, which also meant speeding up the accompanying music track — Fatboy Slim’s “Praise You”— to ensure everything was in sync. The team practiced two days a week, six hours each day to pull it all together.</p><p>On the show, they made full use of the massive stage — jumping, flipping, dive rolling and catapulting across the stage and over fellow team members. Their gravity-defying feats were not lost on the judges, especially Vergara, who gushed, “You literally fly.”</p><p>“They really impressed me as well,” said a chuckling Jesse White, the organization’s 92-year-old founder and the longest-serving (now retired) Illinois Secretary of State.</p><p>But amid the celebration, there was also great sadness, as one of the team’s longtime members, 34-year-old Jeff Williams, died in a motorcycle accident in suburban Mundelein the night before the pretaped audition round aired. McGhee called Williams, whom he trained and mentored, his “little brother/son.” “We talked pretty much every day,” including an hour or so before the accident, he said.</p><p>White released a statement via Instagram honoring Williams, writing in part: “Jeff was a cherished member of the Jesse White Tumbling Team and a dedicated employee in the Illinois Secretary of State’s office. … He will always be a part of the Jesse White Tumbling Team family, and he will be deeply missed.”</p><p>White started the after-school tumbling program in 1959 as a gym show at Tuley Park on the South Side while he was working as an instructor for the Chicago Park District. The organization today also boasts a central hub/training center at the Jesse White Community Center, 412 W. Chicago Ave. More than 18,000 young people have participated in the program over the past 67 years. (They must maintain a “C” average in school and daily school attendance is mandatory.)</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-e80000" name="image-e80000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ed110cb/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F66%2F5c%2F73e2a584406fa4902e85d8a592ac%2Fjessewhitetumblers-260818-10.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/25fb6f4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F66%2F5c%2F73e2a584406fa4902e85d8a592ac%2Fjessewhitetumblers-260818-10.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f4e3988/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F66%2F5c%2F73e2a584406fa4902e85d8a592ac%2Fjessewhitetumblers-260818-10.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Former Illinois Secretary of State Jesse White at the Jesse White Community Center, 412 W. Chicago Ave. in River North, Wednesday, Aug. 12, 2026." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f4e3988/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F66%2F5c%2F73e2a584406fa4902e85d8a592ac%2Fjessewhitetumblers-260818-10.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c159d71/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F66%2F5c%2F73e2a584406fa4902e85d8a592ac%2Fjessewhitetumblers-260818-10.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f4e3988/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F66%2F5c%2F73e2a584406fa4902e85d8a592ac%2Fjessewhitetumblers-260818-10.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Jesse White started the after-school tumbling program in 1959 as a gym show at Tuley Park on the South Side while he was working as an instructor for the Chicago Park District. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“We just want to put these young people on a path by which [they become] a positive force in society,” White said. “I want the kids to move forward in society, to be the kind of individual that all of us can be proud of.”</p><p>While the tumblers have entertained tens of thousands of fans across the globe, White acknowledged there is one special performance invitation they’re hoping — and praying — will come to fruition.</p><p>“Jesse Bianco!” White said with a hearty laugh, in homage to the Italian word for “White” and, of course, a hint to Pope Leo XIV, himself a fellow Chicagoan.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/entertainment-and-culture/2024/11/19/jesse-white-tumblers-chicago-65th-anniversary" >Jesse White Tumblers keep rolling forward after 65 years of local, global shows</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p><i>The team’s first “AGT” live performance airs at 7 p.m. Tuesday on NBC.</i></p><p><i>Interested in trying out for the Jesse White Tumblers in Chicago? The next tryout date is Sept. 12 at the Chicago Avenue location and at Tuley Park, 501 E. 90th Place. Perspective tumblers must be a minimum 6 years old and enrolled in first grade, and possess some basic gymnastics skills.</i></p><p><i>Miriam Di Nunzio is the former Features Editor for the Chicago Sun-Times.</i></p>

entries.title: Photos released of masked dirt-biker sought in Gold Coast hit-and-run
entries.summary: <p>Chicago police released photos of a masked dirt-biker wanted in a hit-and-run in Gold Coast last month that left a woman suffering from 'significant' injuries.</p><p>The crash happened on the Lakefront bike path in the 1400 block of North DuSable Lake Shore Drive around 3:45 p.m. July 20, Chicago police said. </p><p>A 45-year-old woman was cycling on the path when she was struck by a masked male on a yellow dirt bike driving "recklessly," police said. The woman suffered injuries that were considered significant, officials said. </p><p>The dirt bike driver was last seen in the area of Milwaukee and Chicago avenues, police said. </p><p>Anyone with information is asked to contact the Major Accident Investigation Unit at (312) 745-4521 or submit an anonymous tip at CPDTIP.com and use reference # JK346606.<br></p>

entries.title: Girl, 14, grazed in Roseland shooting
entries.summary: <p>A 14-year-old girl is recovering at a hospital after someone shot her in the leg Monday morning in the Roseland neighborhood. </p><p>The girl was in the 300 block of East 103rd Street when someone opened fire and she was grazed in the thigh, police said. </p><p>She was taken to Comer Children's Hospital in good condition. </p><p>No arrests have been made.</p><p>Area 2 detectives are investigating. </p>

He wore an American flag bandana instead of his famous Mandinka-inspired hairstyle, and a single gold crucifix in place of his signature stacked neck chains.</p><p>The 74-year-old superstar and Chicago native threw the ceremonial first pitch at the start of the game, then left Wrigley Field to make an appearance at the Fan Expo Chicago convention in Rosemont.</p><p>The whole day was a treat for those who grew up admiring Mr. T's tough persona as he portrayed Clubber Lang in "Rocky III," B.A. Baracus in "The A-Team" or himself at "WrestleMania." He was quick to offer a photo, handshake, hug or prayer to people, whom he promised to "never let down." His nervousness about performing well was not about vanity, but showing up for his fans.</p><p>"I just want to be good for the people," he said. "I want to be there to uplift them."</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydltitkk-l-tk/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p><b>What advice do you have for someone attending a Crosstown Classic for the first time?</b></p><p><a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" ><i>Reply to this question via email</i></a><i> (please include your first and last name). entries.title: 1 dead, 2 rescued after plunging into Lake Michigan at 31st Street Beach
entries.summary: <p>One man died and another was hurt after slipping under the waters of Lake Michigan near 31st Street beach late Sunday. </p><p>Three men were walking on 31st Street Beach around 11:05 p.m. when they all fell into the water, Chicago police said. </p><p>A witness and Chicago Fire Department personnel pulled the men out of the water, police said. </p><p>One inhaled water and was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center where he died, officials said. A second man also suffered water inhalation and was taken to Insight Hospital where he was in fair condition. </p><p>The third man declined medical attention. </p><p>No further information was immediately available. </p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Mother drowns saving son in Des Plaines River near Libertyville forest preserve
entries.summary: <p>A mother died saving her son who slipped under the waters of the Des Plaines River near a Libertyville forest preserve Sunday night. </p><p>Around 7 p.m., the woman entered the river at Independence Grove to help her son and after helping him reach a family member, she went underwater, the Lake County Forest Preserve said. </p><p>A family member and others nearby helped pull her out and she was taken to the Advocate Condell Medical Center in Libertyville, where she was pronounced dead, officials said. Her name was not released.</p><p>“We are deeply saddened by the tragic death in the Des Plaines River near Libertyville on Sunday evening. Our thoughts are with the victim’s family and loved ones during this incredibly difficult time,” said Ron Davis, Lake County Forest Preserves’ police chief.</p><p>Lake County Forest Preserves Police and the Lake County Medical Examiner’s Office continue to investigate the incident.</p>

entries.title: Cubs' game Saturday will air on Fox Chicago+ because of Bears conflict on Fox 32
entries.summary: <p>When Fox Sports picked up the Cubs’ game Saturday night against the Mariners, it created a conflict for Fox 32 Chicago, which will air the Bears’ preseason game against the Bengals at the same time.</p><p>Fortunately, the local Fox affiliate has an over-the-air sister station for such occurrences.</p><p>WPWR-Channel 50, branded as Fox Chicago+, will carry the Cubs’ game, with pregame coverage beginning at 6 p.m. First pitch is scheduled for 6:15 p.m., with Aaron Goldsmith and John Smoltz on the call for a regional audience.</p><p>WFLD-Channel 32 will carry the Bears’ game, bookended by a pregame show starting at 5 p.m. and a postgame show. The Bears have priority over Fox’s “Baseball Night in America” broadcast — even with the Cubs playing — because of their agreement with Fox 32.</p><p>On most cable systems, Fox Chicago+ is on Ch. 8 in standard definition. In HD, it’s on Xfinity Ch. 184, Astound/RCN Ch. 608 and AT&T U-verse Ch. 1008. The station airs lots of pro sports, including Wolves hockey, Stars soccer and Hounds rugby, as well as college sports.</p><p>Fox’s horse-racing show “Saratoga Saturday” also will move to Fox Chicago+, starting at 5 p.m. and featuring the Alabama Stakes.</p><div class="PageListC" data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-hide-descriptions="true"
