entries.title: La CTA desplegará mediadores contra la violencia y profesionales de salud mental en los trenes este otoño
entries.summary: <p>Docenas de miembros del personal no policial, capacitados para intervenir en episodios de violencia y crisis de salud mental, comenzarán a viajar el próximo mes en las Líneas Roja, Azul y Verde de la Autoridad de Tránsito de Chicago (CTA).</p><p>La junta de la CTA aprobó el miércoles un programa piloto de un año de $10 millones para especialistas en viaje seguro e intervención en crisis, con el fin de complementar el reciente refuerzo de seguridad y la mayor presencia policial en trenes y autobuses.</p><p>Los especialistas, contratados mediante acuerdos con cuatro grupos locales, llevarán chalecos de colores mientras brindan servicios de tratamiento para problemas de salud mental, de conducta y por consumo de drogas a quienes lo necesiten, dijo a la junta Nora Leerhsen, presidenta interina de la CTA.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-b70000" name="module-b70000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>El mayor de los cuatro contratos, por $6.6 millones, fue adjudicado a Metropolitan Family Services, grupo que realiza intervenciones comunitarias contra la violencia en toda la ciudad.</p><p>Dicho grupo proveerá 20 especialistas diarios en intervención contra la violencia comunitaria en la Línea Roja, los siete días de la semana, entre Roosevelt y Lake Street, en dos turnos que abarcan desde el mediodía hasta las 3:30 a.m., dijo a los miembros de la junta Joe Bird, jefe de seguridad de la CTA.</p><p>Leerhsen destacó que el programa piloto se programó a propósito para complementar la "estrategia de seguridad de múltiples capas" de la agencia, que incluyó sumar más policías y alguaciles, lo que ayudó a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/07/09/el-crimen-en-cta-ha-disminuido-los-ultimos-6-meses-consecutivos-segun-la-jefa-de-la-agencia" target="_blank" >registrar una caída del 30% en la delincuencia</a> comparado al año pasado.</p><p>Este nuevo personal no policial ayudará a aliviar parte del trabajo que recientemente ha estado a cargo de la policía.</p><p>"Es un momento increíblemente histórico para la CTA al lanzar estos programas… tras meses de notables aumentos en la presencia policial", dijo Leerhsen.</p><p>Los otros tres contratos se adjudicaron a grupos que suministrarán especialistas en salud mental, en atención a personas sin hogar y en recuperación por abuso de sustancias para las Líneas Verde y Azul.</p><p>Uno de esos grupos, Housing Forward, con sede en Maywood, tiene un contrato por casi $1 millón para proporcionar especialistas en la Línea Verde, de Harlem Avenue a Central Avenue, comentó a la junta Molly Poppe, directora de planificación e innovación de la CTA. Agregó que estarán disponibles de lunes a viernes de 6 p.m. a 1 a.m., y los sábados de 6 p.m. a 11:30 p.m.</p><p>Healthcare Alternative Systems ofrecerá atención de salud conductual bilingüe en el tramo noroeste de la Línea Azul, de O'Hare a Logan Square, dijo Poppe. Dos equipos de dos a tres personas atenderán esos trenes de lunes a viernes, de 9 a.m. a 5 p.m.</p><p>El cuarto grupo, Street Samaritans, tiene un contrato por $1.2 millones para proveer dos equipos de tres personas en el tramo oeste de la Línea Azul, de Austin a Forest Park, dijo Poppe. Cada equipo contará con un clínico de salud mental con licencia y dos especialistas en intervención de crisis capacitados en desescalar situaciones.</p><p>Esta es la primera vez que la CTA emplea oficialmente a interruptores de violencia, sin contar a los “Violence Interrupters” no sancionados, liderados por Tio Hardiman, que han patrullado el tramo sur de la Línea Roja.</p><p>Algunos miembros de la junta de la CTA, que será <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/06/01/nita-rta-transit-law-cta-metra-pace" target="_blank" >reemplazada el próximo mes por nombramientos de la Junta de la Autoridad de Tránsito del Norte de Illinois</a> (NITA), cuestionaron cómo se entrenaría a los interruptores de violencia para decidir si llamar a la policía como refuerzo o no.</p><p>"Su primer objetivo es la desescalada y ofrecer recursos", comentó Bird. "Cuando se convierta en actividad criminal, en una amenaza de violencia, entonces se debe notificar al 911 y a la policía. Pero no antes. Deben actuar de forma independiente".</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Robbins mayor grazed during birthday party at Harold's Chicken restaurant; security fatally shoots gunman
entries.summary: <p>What was supposed to be a birthday celebration at Harold's Chicken Ice Bar in south suburban Robbins quickly turned chaotic after a gunman opened fire and grazed the village's mayor before a security guard fatally shot him. </p><p>Mayor Darren Bryant was at the restaurant in the 13700 block of South Claire Boulevard to celebrate a Robbins resident's birthday just after midnight Saturday when the shooter opened fire, grazing Bryant and wounding a DJ, Sean Howard, a village spokesperson said.</p><p>A security guard then shot the gunman, identified as 29-year-old Marquelle Rose of Chicago, and he was taken to an area hospital where he died, the Cook County sheriff's office said. </p><p>Bryant was taken to an area hospital for "35 minutes max" and returned to the venue to check on patrons after he was released, according to Howard. The DJ was also taken to an area hospital where he was treated and released. </p><p>"He was just there celebrating, awaiting a food order by the way," Howard said. "[He] was there to shake a few hands and thought he would just be going home." </p><p>It isn’t known how many people were inside the restaurant at the time of the shooting, but village officials say many of the individuals inside were seniors. </p><p>The spokesperson noted that Bryant was not the intended target and that the shooting was an isolated incident that "didn’t reflect the progress of Robbins as a town."</p><p>"Robbins had the ugly distinction of being the poorest town in America, and it no longer is," Howard said. "This is just an isolated incident from a guy from Chicago who tried to cause havoc, but we're not going to let it impede the progress of the town." </p><p>Anyone with information on the shooting is encouraged to contact the sheriff's department at 708-865-4896. <br></p>

entries.title: LIV Golf cancels Michigan team event, will end season early
entries.summary: <p>LIV Golf is ending its season one week earlier than planned, announcing Monday it will not hold the team championship in Michigan next week and instead crown the team champion this week in Indiana.</p><p>The 12 tournaments this year — New Orleans was previously postponed — is the shortest schedule for the league since it was launched with massive Saudi Arabia funding in 2022.</p><p>Jon Rahm already has clinched the individual season title for the third straight year. LIV Golf Indianapolis, which starts Thursday at The Club at Chatham Hills, will determine who finishes second and third among players, and the top team.</p><p>The Public Investment Fund of Saudi Arabia, the financial muscle of the rival league from the start, decided in March this would be the final year of funding. LIV Golf announced earlier this month it has an agreement with a lead investor that would sustain a new version of the league for 2027.</p><p>The cancellation of LIV Golf Michigan was not surprising. There have been reports in recent weeks that the tournament has not even started preparing with grandstands and other amenities.</p><p>LIV says tickets will be refunded. It also said it is canceling the entertainment it had lined up for the Indiana event.<br></p>

entries.title: Bears GM Ryan Poles is planning for a good problem to have
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> general manager <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/04/17/bears-nfl-draft-2026-general-manage-ryan-poles-tough-act-follow-pittsburgh-round-1-pick-defensive-end-tackle-thursday" target="_blank" >Ryan Poles</a> knows how to separate business from his personal feelings. But that didn’t make trading receiver DJ Moore easy.</p><p>Poles had insisted Moore be included in what could end up being the signature trade of the GM’s career: a deal with the Panthers that yielded, eventually, quarterback Caleb Williams. Moore and Poles were close during their three years together with the Bears, the last of which was magical.</p><p>When the Bears decided to trade Moore in March to save salary cap space, Poles’ own son was furious at him — until Moore sent him a video message telling him to go easy on his dad. Poles reminded himself that his obligation was to do what was best for the team.</p><p>“I think that takes a little weight off your shoulders,” he said. “Because you did it for the right reason.”</p><p>It won’t be the last difficult decision Poles has to make. That’s the hope, at least.</p><p>Entering his fifth season, Poles is planning ahead in case he has to face a challenge a Bears GM hasn't had to deal with in years: how to keep ascending, and increasingly expensive, players. That includes, if he makes the leap the Bears hope, Williams, who is eligible for a contract extension the minute this season ends.</p><p>Receiver Rome Odunze will be eligible for one then, too. Colston Loveland is two full seasons away, but the Bears think he can be one of the best tight ends in the sport. They’d have to pay him accordingly, the way they did with Darnell Wright earlier this month. They made the former first-round pick the highest-paid right tackle ever.</p><p>Finding a way to keep all of them would be a champagne problem, Poles told the Sun-Times while sitting at a round table in his office last week.</p><p>“I’ll take these problems any day,” he said. “I’ll take them over trading back from [draft pick] No. 1, for sure.”</p><p>Over his shoulder in the distance stood a replica of the Bears’ Super Bowl trophy — and next to it a plastic figurine of a shirtless Ben Johnson that makes Poles smile.</p><p>Looming over all of it, of course, is Williams. His success this year would set the Bears on course for years. The alternative — that Williams joins the list of Bears quarterbacks that have fallen short — would be crushing to the Bears' infrastructure. The Bears need to find out which direction he's headed this year.</p><p>League rules dictate that the Bears can start to negotiate a contract extension with Williams at the end of this season. His four-year rookie deal ends after 2027, though a fifth-year team option would keep him with the Bears through at least 2028. Most elite quarterbacks get an extension done before their fourth season.</p><p>Poles and Johnson believe he’s headed in the right direction, but both want to see him improve before the team commits to him as their quarterback for at least the next half-decade. The Bears want his accuracy to improve and for his heroics to not just be limited to the final two minutes of each game.</p><p>The clues they’ve seen are encouraging. Production, though, will be paramount.</p><p>“You can see Caleb’s desire to get better,” Poles said. “That’s been very high. He’s doubled down on his commitment to the game.”</p><p>Poles traded Moore to clean up their salary cap space not only for 2026, but in the three years afterward. Moore signed a four-year, $110 million extension two years ago — but it kicks in this year. What the Bears saved by trading him can be used to pay at least part of the next big Bears extension. </p><p>Future salaries were part of what kept Poles from going on a high-priced shopping spree this offseason. He was tempted to ride the momentum of the Bears’ first playoff win in 15 years, but reminded himself he wanted to contend for more than just a season or two.</p><p>“When you get into player acquisition phases, whether it’s free agency or the draft, we’re all like kids in a candy store,” he said. “But we surround ourselves with structure. … </p><p>"We want to do some unique things here and have success for a long time. That absolutely has to be a part of the process.”</p><p>Moore was the best player a contending Bears team has traded away since the start of the Phil Emery era. If the Bears keep growing, he won’t be the last. </p><p>Poles knows the biases that can come with evaluating his own players. But he figures he knows them better than anyone else, too. Poles has studied what the Patriots — and even last year’s champion, the Seahawks — did with their salary structures. He lived it in Kansas City as a member of the Chiefs front office when they gave Patrick Mahomes a 10-year, $450 million extension — and had to find a way to afford it.</p><p>The Bears hope to have anything close to resembling those problems one day. Poles, at least, is preparing a plan for them.</p><p>“It does get harder,” he said.</p><p></p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" entries.title: Bears sign DE Marcus Davenport
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> signed veteran edge rusher Marcus Davenport, a former first-round pick, to a one-year deal Monday.</p><p>Davenport, whom Saints made him the 14th pick of the 2018 draft, figures to be a depth piece. Despite starting seven games for the Lions last year, Davenport didn't put up strong pass rush statistics. He ranked 103rd out of 115 edge rushers graded by Pro Football Focus. He had nine sacks in 2021 and a total of four in the four seasons since.</p><p>He knows the Bears, though. Defensive coordinator Dennis Allen coached him in New Orleans and Ben Johnson was on the Lions staff in 2024 when he played there. The Bears brought Davenport in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/16/bears-training-camp-former-first-round-pick-marcus-davenport-visits-defensive-end-needy" target="_blank" >for a visit </a>Sunday. </p><p>The Bears' top three defensive ends during training camp have been Montez Sweat, Austin Booker and Dayo Odeyingbo. Sweat returned to practice Sunday after missing 10 days due to injury. The team plans to use Odeyingbo at defensive tackle on certain passing downs.</p><p>To make room, the Bears waived tight end Nikola Kalinic with an injury designation after he hurt his knee in the first quarter Saturday. Running back Coleman Bennett was waived. They also signed Deantre Prince, who played for the UFL's Louisville Kings this year.</p><p></p><p></p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" entries.title: Gobernador de Illinois firma ley para ayudar a dueños de casa afectados por las inundaciones
entries.summary: <p>Los dueños de casa de Illinois afectados por inundaciones causadas por las poderosas tormentas que azotaron el estado recibirán ayuda para la recuperación mediante un nuevo programa firmado por el gobernador de Illinois, JB Pritzker.</p><p>Las fuertes tormentas y las inundaciones en todo el estado han llevado a los legisladores a facilitar los esfuerzos de ayuda, según la oficina del gobernador.</p><p>Tras la firma del Proyecto de Ley del Senado 3925 como ley el viernes, los dueños de casa del estado podrán participar en programas de ayuda ante desastres que normalmente no están cubiertos por las pólizas de seguro estándar.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-7e0000" name="module-7e0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>“El verano pasado, las fuertes tormentas e inundaciones golpearon comunidades en todo Illinois, dejando a familias trabajadoras con miles de dólares en gastos inesperados”, dijo Pritzker en un comunicado de su oficina. Con la nueva ley, “estamos dando a las comunidades otra herramienta para ayudar a los propietarios a recuperarse. Cuando Washington se niega a ayudar, seguiremos luchando por ustedes mientras encontramos maneras de ayudarnos unos a otros”.</p><p>Bajo la nueva ley, el <a class="Link" href="https://swhomeequity.com/en-espanol" target="_blank" >Southwest Equity Home Assurance Program</a> y el <a class="Link" href="https://nwheap.com/es/" target="_blank" >Northwest Home Equity Assurance Program</a> podrán establecer normativa que amplíe la Ley de Garantía de la Plusvalía Inmobiliaria.</p><p>Un programa temporal de reembolsos directos por daños por inundación de tres años estará disponible para los propietarios, y los hogares elegibles recibirán un reembolso único de hasta el 50% de los gastos relacionados con inundaciones, con un reembolso máximo de $1,000, según el comunicado.</p><p>Estos programas de ayuda llegan en un contexto en el que el gobierno federal se niega a ayudar con la recuperación tras desastres naturales, destacó la oficina del gobernador en el comunicado.</p><p>En 2025, dos tormentas trajeron <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago/2025/08/26/city-issues-disaster-proclamation-for-areas-affected-by-rain-flooding" target="_blank" >fuertes lluvias e inundaciones repentinas</a> a partes del sur, suroeste y oeste de Chicago, pero la administración de Trump no proporcionó asistencia de la Agencia Federal para el Manejo de Emergencias (FEMA), dijo el comunicado.</p><p>En ese momento, Pritzker <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/02/10/administracion-de-trump-niega-la-apelacion-de-ayuda-de-illinois-por-los-desastres-de-las-tormentas-de-verano" target="_blank" >aseguró que las denegaciones</a> fueron motivadas políticamente porque el presidente aprobó asistencia similar a otros estados, como Dakota del Norte y Alaska.</p><p>“Al final del día, se trata de lo mismo que siempre hemos buscado: mantener la propiedad de la vivienda y estabilizar nuestros vecindarios”, dijo Victoria Gaspar, directora ejecutiva del Southwest Home Equity Assurance Program, en el comunicado.</p><p>“Las inundaciones pueden ser una de las cosas más disruptivas y costosas que enfrenta un dueño de casa, y este proyecto de ley nos da una herramienta real para ayudar a nuestros miembros a recuperarse y quedarse. Programas como este, hogar por hogar, son los que mantienen fuertes a nuestros vecindarios”.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: DUI, reckless homicide charges approved for driver in fatal Stevenson wreck near Bridgeport
entries.summary: <p>A 20-year-old Chicago man has been released from a hospital and charged with reckless homicide and aggravated driving under the influence after a weekend crash on the Stevenson Expressway that left him injured and his passenger dead.</p><p>About 4:30 a.m. in the southbound lanes near Wentworth Avenue, Armando Gonzalez Vargas was behind the wheel of a white GMC that rear-ended another SUV, causing Vargas' GMC to run off the road and slam into a concrete median barrier, state police said. </p><p>Carlos E. Vazquez, 26 and of Chicago, was a passenger in the GMC, was pronounced deceased on scene, according to state police, who said Gonzalez Vargas was taken to an area hospital with injuries. </p><p>The driver and passenger of the SUV were also transported to an area hospital with injuries, state police said. </p><p>Sunday, he was released from the hospital and charged, state police said. <br></p>

entries.title: Ohio State, Oregon lead AP preseason Top 25
entries.summary: <p>Ohio State and Oregon were 1-2 in The Associated Press Top 25 released Monday, giving the Big Ten Conference the top two teams in the preseason rankings for the first time in 65 years and just the second time ever.</p><p>The Buckeyes received 40 first-place votes and Oregon received 14 in voting by 69 media members who cover college football.</p><p>Ohio State will go into a season No. 1 for the ninth time, and first since 2015. The Buckeyes are now tied with Alabama for second-most preseason No. 1 rankings behind Oklahoma's 10.</p><p>Oregon has its highest preseason ranking in program history after having opened No. 3 four times.</p><p>Georgia, Notre Dame and Texas round out the top five. Defending national champion Indiana starts at No. 6 and is followed by Miami, Texas A&M, Mississippi and Oklahoma.</p><p>Notre Dame received six first-place votes, Indiana got eight and Miami one.</p><p>This is the first year a conference has held down the top two spots in the preseason poll since Oklahoma and Nebraska of the Big Eight were 1-2 in 1987.</p><p>The last time the Big Ten had the Nos. 1 and 2 teams in the preseason was 1961, when Iowa and Ohio State topped the poll. The Hawkeyes lost four of their last five games after a 4-0 start and finished that season unranked. The Buckeyes went 8-0-1 and ended the season No. 2 behind unbeaten Alabama.</p><p>The Big Ten has won three straight College Football Playoff championships (Michigan, Ohio State, Indiana) and will be going for an unprecedented fourth straight national title. This is the fourth consecutive year the Big Ten has had two of the top three teams in the preseason rankings.</p><p>The Southeastern Conference leads all conferences with nine teams in the preseason Top 25, marking the third straight year it has had at least that many. Five of the top 10 teams are from the SEC for the first time since 2013.</p><p>Four Big 12 teams are ranked, with conference champion Texas Tech the highest at No. 12. The Atlantic Coast Conference has three ranked teams, with the Hurricanes joined by No. 19 SMU and No. 24 Louisville. There are no Group of Six schools in the Top 25.</p><h3>Top-ranked Buckeyes</h3><h3></h3><p>The offense is loaded. Heisman Trophy finalist Julian Sayin was the most accurate passer in the nation by a wide margin last season, Jeremiah Smith leads the nation in receiving yards and receiving touchdowns over the last two years and Bo Jackson is coming off a 1,000-yard rushing season as a freshman.</p><p>There is little concern about the defense even though eight starters must be replaced for a second straight year. At least six transfers are projected to start or play major roles.</p><p>Ohio State will get tested early and often. The Buckeyes visit Texas on Sept. 12 and five of their nine conference games are against preseason ranked teams, including at Indiana and against Oregon at home.</p><p>The Buckeyes have ended a season No. 1 in the AP poll six times (1942, 1954, 1968, 2002, 2014, 2024).</p><h3>Bulldogs best of the SEC</h3><h3></h3><p>The beat goes on for Kirby Smart's Georgia Bulldogs. They're in the preseason top five for the ninth straight year. The two-time defending SEC champion Bulldogs are favored to play in a sixth straight conference title game and appear in the CFP for the sixth time in 10 years.</p><p>Texas, the preseason No. 1 last year, opens in the top five for the third straight year. No. 8 Texas A&M is in the preseason top 10 for the first time since it was No. 6 in 2022, the year that marked the beginning of the end for coach Jimbo Fisher.</p><p>Pete Golding's first full season as Mississippi head coach starts with the No. 9 Rebels in the preseason top 10 for the second time in three years and third time since 1970. No. 10 Oklahoma is in the preseason top 10 for the first time since 2022, when it was in the Big 12.</p><h3>What about the Hoosiers?</h3><h3></h3><p>Indiana is the seventh returning national champion in 40 years, and second in three years, to be ranked outside the top five in the preseason (Michigan went into the 2024 season ranked No. 9 after winning the national title).</p><p>The Hoosiers became the first team in the modern era to go 16-0, and they return lots of talent and signed a top-10 transfer class. The move from Heisman Trophy winner and No. 1 NFL draft pick Fernando Mendoza to TCU transfer Josh Hoover at quarterback apparently put doubts in the minds of voters.</p><h3>Poll nuggets</h3><p>• Ohio State will try to become the 12th team to start and finish No. 1 since the AP preseason poll debuted in 1950. The last team to do it was Alabama in 2017.</p><p>• Notre Dame has its highest preseason ranking since it was No. 2 in 2006. The Fighting Irish, who have a Heisman candidate in quarterback CJ Carr, bring a 10-game winning streak into the season and are still smarting from being left out of the playoff.</p><p>• Lane Kiffin's first LSU team is No. 11 after finishing 7-6 and unranked under Brian Kelly and Frank Wilson.</p><p>• Ten of the 12 CFP teams last season are ranked. The two that aren't are James Madison and Tulane from the Group of Six.</p><p>• No. 23 Houston has its first preseason ranking in four years and third since 1991.</p><p></p><p></p><h3>The Top 25</h3><p>1. Ohio State (40 first-place votes) </p><p>2. Oregon (14) </p><p>3. Georgia </p><p>4. Notre Dame (6) </p><p>5. Texas 0-0 </p><p>6. Indiana (8) </p><p>7. Miami (FL) (1)</p><p>8. Texas A&M </p><p>9. Ole Miss</p><p>10. Oklahoma </p><p>11. LSU 0-0 </p><p>12. Texas Tech</p><p>13. Alabama </p><p>14. BYU </p><p>14. USC </p><p>16. Michigan</p><p>17. Washington </p><p>18. Penn State </p><p>19. SMU </p><p>20. Tennessee </p><p>21. Utah </p><p>22. Iowa </p><p>23. Houston </p><p>24. Louisville </p><p>25. Missouri </p><p>Others receiving votes: Clemson 112, Florida 51, Boise State 43, Arizona 32, TCU 11, Navy 10, South Carolina 10, Illinois 9, Oklahoma State 8, Vanderbilt 8, Pittsburgh 7, Virginia Tech 6, Minnesota 5, UNLV 4, New Mexico 4, Georgia Tech 4, James Madison 3, Auburn 3, Memphis 2, California 2, Liberty 1, Western Michigan 1, Tulane 1, Virginia 1</p>

entries.title: Debt-laden Bally’s future in ‘substantial doubt’ amid video gambling dispute over Chicago casino
entries.summary: <p>Bally’s has acknowledged its massive debt creates “substantial doubt about its ability to continue” over the next year, when the company is supposed to open its long-delayed Chicago casino complex in River West.</p><p>The statement of “going concern” was included in Friday’s quarterly filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission from Bally’s, which says it “is pursuing a number of financing alternatives intended to enhance its liquidity, including asset monetization, an equity sale and debt financing.”</p><p>The disclosure comes as Bally’s butts heads with City Council members who authorized video gambling terminals that the company says will eat away its revenue — providing fodder for Council members who <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/08/12/ballys-permanent-casino-river-west-construction-slowdown-council-members-letter" target="_blank" ><u>argue that’s just an excuse</u></a> to slow down a project Bally’s can’t afford to complete.</p><p>Companies are required to issue going-concern warnings if there’s “substantial doubt” about their ability to avoid defaulting on debt over the next 12 months.</p><p>Bally’s cited a series of “adverse conditions” its Chicago operation faces, including the fact it has weathered “significant losses and negative cash flows from operations since its inception and expects to continue to incur such losses and negative cash flows for the foreseeable future.”</p><p>While the company is on the hook for about $400 million in costs over the next two years to complete its permanent complex at 777 W. Chicago Ave., Bally’s still isn’t breaking even at its temporary casino at the historic Medinah Temple, 600 N. Wabash Ave., which opened about three years ago.</p><p>The company ran a loss of $56.4 million over the first half of 2026 and has an accumulated deficit of $233.3 million, Bally’s reported.</p><p>But company officials say that’s “entirely separate from, and unrelated to” Bally’s decision to slow down construction of the hotel, event center and other amenities adjacent to its casino project, which has been beset by financing and logistical delays.</p><p>Bally’s announced last week it was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/09/ballys-to-stop-work-on-some-amenities-at-permanent-chicago-casino-development-amid-video-gambling-dispute" target="_blank" ><u>stopping much of that ancillary work</u></a> in response to the city’s approval of video gambling terminals that were allowed to help balance last year’s city budget in defiance of Mayor Brandon Johnson and Bally’s host community agreement.</p><p>Johnson’s administration has yet to license any of the bars, restaurants and other establishments that already have state approval to plug in slot machines.</p><p>A Bally’s spokesperson said in an email that “there has been no change to the status of Bally’s Chicago’s construction” and maintained the company “remains well situated to continue delivering on its obligations.”</p><p>“The going concern disclosure is based on a forward-looking technical accounting analysis which considers only funding that has been unconditionally secured as of the date of the assessment,” according to the company. “Bally’s Chicago has consistently demonstrated its ability to execute this project, including advancing construction ahead of the original Host Community Agreement deliverable timeline. We remain focused and committed to opening the permanent casino in early 2027.”</p><p>But the disclosure supports the argument of Bally’s City Council detractors, including 42nd Ward Ald. Brendan Reilly, who told the Chicago Sun-Times last week the company was “trying to turn lemons into lemonade by blaming VGT as the reason they’re slowing down construction.”</p><p>“They’ve told their own investors that they are heavily leveraged and have over $5 billion in debt, and that encumbrance could have a negative impact on their future operations,” Reilly said.</p><p>He was among 28 aldermen who signed a letter calling for Bally’s officials to resume all work and appear for a public hearing on their progress.</p><p>Bally’s spokesperson said: “We continue to stand ready to engage in open, honest and collaborative conversation about the risks to the City’s finances, police and fire pension funds, union jobs and public safety because of the legalization of video gambling terminals.”</p>
entries.author: Mitchell Armentrout

entries.title: Three ways the Sky can make the most of their last nine games
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> still want to make a playoff push, even as the odds approach impossible. The commitment is admirable. For coach Tyler Marsh, it might even feel personal. Coaches operate on short leashes in the WNBA, and he's nearing the end of his second losing season.</p><p>But the better move is to play the odds. The playoffs aren't happening. That doesn't mean there's nothing left to accomplish.</p><p>The Sky have promising young talent beyond marquee names like Rickea Jackson and Kamilla Cardoso, and a month left to experiment with how the pieces fit long-term.</p><p>In that spirit, here are three things I'd like to see from Marsh and Co. in the final nine games.</p><h3><b>1. More role definition for Jacy Sheldon</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Why did the Sky trade a 2028 first-round pick for Sheldon?</p><p>It's still not entirely clear. Sheldon is unselfish, high-motor and willing to do whatever coaches ask. But when you ask a player to do everything, sometimes you get nothing in particular.</p><p>The simplest way to start defining her role is as a 3-and-D guard. In 18 games as a starter, Sheldon is shooting 40% from 3-point range and averaging 1.2 steals. And yet she's hesitated all season, taking two or fewer 3-pointers in 14 games.</p><p>Marsh should make it a rule: Her minutes depend on taking at least three a game.</p><p>Then she can build from there. Sheldon has scorer's tools — speed in transition, a nice finishing package and a pull-up jumper. She just needs the mindset to match.</p><p>She told the Sun-Times last week that she grew up idolizing Kelsey Mitchell and counts Devin Booker and Tyrese Maxey among her favorites on the men's side. Marsh needs to get her hunting shots the way they do.</p><h3><b>2. More minutes for Gabriela Jaquez</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Rookie Gabriela Jaquez has had two different seasons.</p><p>She introduced herself with a bang, averaging 9.2 points and 4.3 rebounds while shooting 35% from 3-point range in her first 15 games. Since then, she has faded from view.</p><p>In August, Jaquez is averaging about two points in 11 minutes per game.</p><p>So which came first: Did her confidence drop because her minutes waned, or did the minutes disappear because the confidence dropped?</p><p>The Sky might as well find out by giving her more minutes. There was a perfect opening with starting shooting guard Sydney Taylor sidelined by a groin injury, but most of the extra guard minutes have gone to veteran Rachel Banham.</p><p>To Banham's credit, she has made the most of them, hitting 11 of 28 3-pointers over the last five games. But the Sky used the No. 5 pick on Jaquez because they believe she can help anchor their future. Banham's contract expires after this season.</p><p>The long view should take precedence.</p><h3><b>3. More outside shooting for Aicha Coulibaly</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Marsh was asked recently for a player comparison for Aicha Coulibaly and pointed to former Sky forward Michaela Onyenwere. Both are athletic, high-motor wings with the strength and versatility to play the 3 or the 4.</p><p>There is one big difference: Onyenwere has developed into a nearly 40% 3-point shooter. Coulibaly has made one 3-pointer all season.</p><p>So that's the next step. Coulibaly is already one of the league's better development stories, hustling her way onto a standard contract and making her living with her strength and physicality on defense.</p><p>That same force translates offensively. She gets downhill, draws contact and attacks the glass. But teams leave her wide open on the perimeter, so she should start letting it fly. She knows it, too, and regularly stays after practice to work on her shot.</p><p>"My shot, I just gotta take it," Coulibaly told the Sun-Times last week. "I don't take enough to show that I can shoot it."</p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" entries.title: Thousands of Gary residents still without power after last week's deadly storms
entries.summary: <p>Thousands of Gary residents remained without power Monday after last week’s storms wreaked havoc on northwest Indiana.</p><p>While Monday was the first day without rain in over a week, several downed trees still littered Gary’s streets. Most stoplights were out. Several crews worked on power lines and residents cleaned outside their homes and in their yards.</p><p>Kimberly Guajardo, who has lived in Gary for over 20 years, said she and her husband have been without power since Aug. 11. Several large trees on their property were knocked over or were missing large branches. They had sheltered in their basement during the worst of the storm with their daughter and three grandchildren. </p><p>"We're alive and we have a home," said Guajardo, standing among the debris in her front yard. "I know a lot of people that have lost their entire homes. I've got loved ones that their houses had to be demolished. They lost everything they had."</p><p>Their generator wasn't working, but they said they were grateful to have running water. </p><p>Several Gary residents, including Guajardo's sister, use well water, which requires power to pump water through a home's pipes. Her sister has come by each day to collect water in plastic jugs. Guajardo has a solar-powered battery to charge her phone and coolers to keep their food fresh. They use candles to light their home. </p><p>"We're living in the 1700s but we're making it work," she said. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> And people are handling the devastation from the storms differently, she said. Some are lending a helping hand to their neighbors, while others are arguing on Facebook or getting in fights in long lines at gas stations. </p><p>"We just have to come together as a community and try to help each other the best we can and get through this best we can," said Guajardo, who was born in Chicago and grew up in Alabama. "Right now is not the time to argue. It's the time to come together and get things done." </p><p>As of Monday afternoon, over 100,000 Indiana residents were still without power, according to the state's utility company NIPSCO. entries.title: Cubs send Dansby Swanson, Edward Cabrera to IL as key injuries pop up in middle of playoff race
entries.summary: <p>Things were feeling a lot like May and June on Monday at Wrigley Field, with ample injury news and the Crosstown-rival White Sox on the schedule, challenging for intra-city supremacy.</p><p>While the Wrigleyville buzz was about a rare late-season clash between playoff-dreaming teams from both sides of town, the Cubs were hit with bigger-picture problems, sending their starting shortstop and their big offseason trade acquisition to the injured list in the middle of a playoff race.</p><p>After he <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/16/cubs-shortstop-dansby-swanson-leaves-game-with-apparent-injury" >left Sunday’s game following an uncomfortable swing</a>, the Cubs learned shortstop Dansby Swanson has a left oblique strain, one that manager Craig Counsell said is expected to keep the shortstop out for four weeks.</p><p>The Cubs are confident they’ll get Swanson — a Gold Glove defender who ranked fourth on the team with 18 homers coming into Monday — back for the home stretch of the regular season and the playoffs, but they’ll have to figure out a way to keep their best-in-baseball defense humming without him.</p><p>The everyday shortstop job will go to second baseman Nico Hoerner in the meantime, with reserve infielder Pedro Ramirez taking over everyday duties at second base.</p><p>Hoerner will have to reacclimate himself to shortstop; he came into Monday with only 36 appearances there in the last three seasons. Ramirez, meanwhile, will get to show what he can do as an everyday player after hitting .299/.353/.441 in his first 140 big league plate appearances as a part-time player.</p><p>“Pedro’s a good player, bottom line,” Counsell said. “I told you out of spring training, if Pedro has to come and play every day in April, I’m good with it. This is after 130 major league at-bats where he’s really performed. He’s more than ready for this.”</p><p>Utility man Matt Shaw, who’s had <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/11/cubs-matt-shaw-injury-hand-sprain-injured-list-rehab-shota-imanaga-home-runs-nationals-edward-cabrera-daniel-palencia" >his own lengthy IL stay with a nagging hand sprain</a>, could return soon, with Counsell saying a good day Monday could lead to the start of a minor league rehab assignment later this week.</p><p>Swanson’s absence will be one of the few to affect a Cubs position player this season, with the vast majority of the team’s injuries — and there have been a lot of them — impacting the pitching staff.</p><p>The hurlers couldn’t avoid further misfortune Monday, though, with righty starter Edward Cabrera going to the IL with a blister on a finger on his throwing hand.</p><p>Cabrera — who the Cubs dealt for in the winter, sending top-rated outfield prospect Owen Caissie to the Marlins in a win-now move — was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/16/cubs-stagger-into-white-sox-series-after-losing-dansby-swanson-and-seeing-edward-cabrera-get-rocked" >roughed up in his return</a> from a nearly two-month absence Sunday, surrendering seven runs to the rival Cardinals in his first major league outing since suffering a hamstring injury in late June.</p><p>It’s been a question <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/07/cubs-edward-cabrera-starting-rotation-bullpen-playoffs-craig-counsell-tommy-hottovy-mlb-trade-deadline-jed-hoyer" >how Cabrera would fit into a suddenly overcrowded Cubs rotation</a> following the front office’s trades for righties Kevin Gausman and Clay Holmes at the deadline earlier this month. Most baseball folks, Counsell included, would have told you that this stuff tends to figure itself out, and indeed, it seems Cabrera might have made his final start of the season.</p><p>The team has a “working plan” to bring him back from this injury as a bullpen arm, seeing a possible trend that blisters — which sent him to the IL earlier this season, too — seem to be affecting him during longer outings. Shorter stints, like those by bullpen arms, could be a solution to keeping him healthy enough to pitch.</p><p>“We’re hoping can have the blister behind us,” Counsell said. “He’s dealt with this and pitched with this. One of the things we’re thinking: It doesn’t pop up, necessarily, in bullpens, when the volume is lower. Maybe we can make some progress there, and that can be a fix, at least, for the last six weeks here.”</p><p>“A hundred percent I’d go to the bullpen,” Cabrera said through an interpreter Monday. “The important thing is to be here and to be able to help the team. If they were to ask me to come out of the bullpen, I’d happily do it.”</p><p>But Cabrera has struggled to be effective whenever he’s been on the mound this season, the owner of an ugly 5.68 ERA after Sunday’s troublesome start.</p><p>“It hasn’t clicked,” Counsell said. “I wish every story was a success story. This one, right now, is not. We’re going to keep working on trying to find answers there and trying to find solutions. It’s something that’s very important.”</p><p>“When things are going well, you’re not really worried about anything else,” Cabrera said. “But whenever you start thinking that things aren’t necessarily going as well, that’s the time where you have to keep working.”</p><p>Cabrera was reinserted into the Cubs’ rotation upon his Sunday return. This IL trip creates a new opening, perhaps easily filled by the return of lefty David Peterson, who was moved to the bullpen Sunday. Counsell said that decision will come later.</p><p>The Cubs brought Javier Assad back from Triple-A Iowa a day after Cabrera took his roster spot. Additionally, reserve infielder Owen Miller and outfielder Kevin Alcantara came up from the minors, with infielder James Triantos going down to the I-Cubs.</p><p></p><p></p><bsp-listcarousel entries.title: Los campos de concentración de estadounidenses de origen japonés resuena en las políticas actuales
entries.summary: <p>El temor tras el ataque japonés a Pearl Harbor llevó a la firma de la <a class="Link" href="https://www.archives.gov/milestone-documents/executive-order-9066" target="_blank" >Orden Ejecutiva 9066</a> el 19 de febrero de 1942, que permitió la remoción forzada de todas las personas de ascendencia japonesa de sus hogares en la Costa Oeste de los Estados Unidos y su traslado a centros de ensamblaje y campos de concentración.</p><p>Los 10 campos de concentración que se construyeron recluyeron a 126,000 japoneses, dos tercios de ellos ciudadanos estadounidenses.</p><p>El <a class="Link" href="https://savingplaces.org/places/tule-lake" target="_blank" >Tule Lake</a> Segregation Center fue el campo más grande. Albergó a 18,700 adultos y niños en un espacio sórdido y hacinado diseñado para 15,000 internos. Apenas el mes pasado, la organización sin fines de lucro Tule Lake Committee realizó su peregrinación bianual de cuatro días a Tule Lake, California, para descendientes y sobrevivientes de este oscuro capítulo de la historia estadounidense.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-eb0000" name="module-eb0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Hacia el final de la guerra, en Tule Lake el Departamento de Justicia puso en marcha un plan sin precedentes que permitió la deportación de estadounidenses de origen japonés considerados "desleales". La Ley Pública 78-805 se redactó el 1 de julio de 1944 y permitió a ciudadanos estadounidenses renunciar a su ciudadanía.</p><p>Muchos estadounidenses de origen japonés fueron engañados, creyendo que si renunciaban a su ciudadanía, sus familias podrían permanecer unidas bajo custodia protectora en Tule Lake. Horriblemente, la desinformación llevó a 5,461 estadounidenses de origen japonés a renunciar a su ciudadanía por nacimiento, que parecía no tener valor, en Tule Lake.</p><p>Sin la protección de la ciudadanía estadounidense, varios miles de jóvenes fueron separados de sus familias, clasificados como "extranjeros enemigos" e internados y deportados a campos de internamiento del Departamento de Justicia. La decisión de renunciar a la ciudadanía por nacimiento fue un acto realizado bajo presión y casi todos los que renunciaron buscaron la restitución de su ciudadanía, que el Departamento de Justicia se negó a otorgar.</p><p>Afortunadamente, el abogado de derechos civiles <a class="Link" href="http://remembrance-project.janm.org/tributes/wayne-collins.html" target="_blank" >Wayne M. Collins</a>, a través de su defensa, detuvo las deportaciones involuntarias y restituyó la ciudadanía a casi todos los estadounidenses de origen japonés que habían sido despojados de su derecho de nacimiento. Pero a pesar de la reversión de las deportaciones, quienes renunciaron a su ciudadanía se enfrentaron a décadas de vergüenza y rechazo en la comunidad japonesa.</p><p>Cuatro décadas y seis años después del encarcelamiento en tiempos de guerra, nuestro gobierno <a class="Link" href="https://www.archives.gov/press/press-releases/2013/nr13-118.html" target="_blank" >reconoció el error de sus acciones</a> con una disculpa presidencial, indemnizaciones y pagos de reparación a los sobrevivientes.</p><p>Las deportaciones masivas de hoy, las condiciones inhumanas de detención y los ataques a la ciudadanía por nacimiento recuerdan el trato injusto que sufrieron los estadounidenses de origen japonés durante la Segunda Guerra Mundial. ¿Cuándo dejaremos de cometer los mismos gravísimos errores?.</p><p><i>Michael Harada, Wilmette </i></p><p><i>Barbara Takei, Sacramento, California </i></p><h3>Apuntando alto para el Departamento de Recursos Naturales del estado</h3><p>El gobernador JB Pritzker ha construido uno de los <a class="Link" href="https://rmi.org/resources/state-climate-action-updated-scorecards-tracking-progress-to-2030/" target="_blank" >expedientes de acción climática más sólidos del país</a> y ahora tiene la oportunidad de hacerlo aún más sólido.</p><p>Una naturaleza sana y resiliente es una parte clave de la ecuación, que puede atraer más inversión económica. Un nombramiento transformador para el próximo director del <a class="Link" href="https://dnr.illinois.gov/" target="_blank" >Departamento de Recursos Naturales de Illinois</a> (IDNR) puede extender su liderazgo mediante inversiones visionarias en la naturaleza.</p><p>La misión del departamento es administrar los recursos naturales del estado para la salud de los ecosistemas y el bienestar de los residentes. Eso va más allá de los parques estatales e incluye garantizar que todas las tierras y aguas de Illinois sean saludables y hermosas.</p><p>La gente elige dónde vivir en función de la calidad de vida. El acceso a parques, senderos, agua limpia y áreas naturales vibrantes es precisamente lo que hace que un lugar sea atractivo. Es por eso que las familias echan raíces y por qué los jóvenes profesionales optan por una ciudad en lugar de otra. Las empresas también lo saben. Cuando deciden dónde ubicarse y cómo atraer talento, buscan lugares donde sus empleados quieran vivir.</p><p>Como expresidenta del Consejo de Conservación y Políticas de los Refugios Forestales del Condado de Cook, vi de primera mano cómo un buen liderazgo puede proteger la tierra y las comunidades locales. Deer Grove East Forest Preserve es una de esas historias de éxito.</p><p>Un <a class="Link" href="https://openlands.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/rpt_dge_econ_valuation_final_10102016.pdf" target="_blank" >análisis económico del trabajo de restauración</a> encontró que cada dólar invertido en restauración generó un retorno inmediato de $2 en empleos y actividad económica. A largo plazo, produjo un impresionante retorno de $6 por el control de inundaciones, los beneficios de la calidad del agua y la actividad recreativa. A escala estatal, los beneficios para la salud y la economía de este tipo de conservación son indiscutibles.</p><p>Los votantes del Condado de Cook lo entienden y respondieron en 2022 aprobando, con una mayoría abrumadora, <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagotribune.com/2023/10/17/cook-county-forest-preserves-189-million-budget-marks-new-era-with-referendum-cash/" target="_blank" >una medida en la boleta</a> que aumenta la inversión en la naturaleza en $45 millones al año. Los cinco condados periféricos siguieron el ejemplo en 2024, generando más de $1,000 millones durante los próximos 20 años para la naturaleza.</p><p>Aquí hay un verdadero margen de crecimiento. Illinois ha perdido más del 99% de la pradera original del estado y más del 85% de sus humedales históricos y ocupa el puesto 49 a nivel nacional en áreas naturales protegidas por habitante, un claro indicador de hábitats fragmentados. A medida que el cambio climático remodela los ecosistemas en todo el país, Illinois tiene la oportunidad de dar un paso al frente y liderar.</p><p>Amamos el Estado de la Pradera. El gobernador también lo ama. Un nombramiento transformador para el Departamento de Recursos Naturales de Illinois es su oportunidad de escribir el siguiente capítulo de ese legado.</p><p><i>Wendy J. Paulson, presidenta ejecutiva, Bobolink Foundation </i></p><h3>Trump no merece que le llamen líder</h3><p>Cuestiono el reciente artículo de opinión de David McGrath titulado <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/other-views/2026/07/31/president-donald-trump-cold-blooded-leader-death-iran-ice-shootings-covid-measles-david-mcgrath" target="_blank" >“Trump es nuestro líder de sangre fría”</a>. No cuestiono las atrocidades y la ilegalidad que McGrath señaló en la administración de Trump. Sin embargo, no estoy de acuerdo con que se describa a Trump como un "líder" .</p><p>Según Merriam-Webster, liderazgo significa "el cargo o la posición de un líder", "la capacidad de liderar" y "el acto o la instancia de liderar". No logro ver ninguna cualidad de "liderazgo", ni integridad, honestidad, responsabilidad, rendición de cuentas, empatía o compasión en Trump, dado que ha llevado al país al borde económico con sus aranceles, nos ha puesto en peligro en una guerra sin posibilidad de victoria en el Medio Oriente y menospreció la educación superior y la ciencia como bases del gobierno.</p><p>Las palabras tienen significado, como seguramente sabe McGrath. Creo que debemos ser cuidadosos al llamar a Trump un "líder" . Yo lo describo como el "ocupante" de la Casa Blanca, pero dejaré en manos del profesor McGrath encontrar un apelativo o epíteto más apropiado.</p><p><i>Linda Hendelman, West Ridge</i></p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: Buss family will sell its minority stake in Lakers to new majority owners Josh Kushner and Bob Iger
entries.summary: <p>LOS ANGELES — The Buss family has voted to sell its 17.8% minority ownership of the Los Angeles Lakers to new majority owners Josh Kushner and Bob Iger, ESPN and The Athletic are reporting.</p><p>The decision Monday by the six children of late owner Jerry Buss will end the family's 47 years in an ownership role with the 17-time NBA champion franchise. The move also appears to end Jeanie Buss' tenure as the Lakers' governor.</p><p>"We have decided as a family to sell the remaining Buss Family Trust shares to the Bob Iger group as part of the ongoing transaction," the Buss family said in a statement issued to ESPN. "We love the Lakers, Laker fans and will continue to support Los Angeles, but it is time to use this opportunity to move on and exit gracefully while we still can."</p><p>Jeanie Buss, the Lakers' governor since Jerry Buss' death in 2013, led the family's decision to sell a controlling stake in the Lakers to Dodgers owner Mark Walter last year at a valuation of $10 billion.</p><p>Not all of the six Buss siblings — Jeanie, Jim, Johnny, Janie, Joey and Jesse — were in favor of the deal despite retaining their family trust's minority ownership stake, and Joey and Jesse were fired from their front-office jobs with the team last November.</p><p>The siblings have been in frequent conflict since their father's death, with Jeanie firing Jim from his job as the Lakers' head of basketball operations in 2017, followed a week later with a lawsuit against her brothers amid an attempt by Jim and Johnny to oust Jeanie from her role as the Lakers' controlling owner.</p><p>Walter, who is under federal investigation for tax issues, abruptly reached a deal earlier this month to flip the Lakers to Kushner and Iger at a valuation of $12.5 billion, another record for a pro sports team. Venture capitalist Kushner and former Disney CEO Iger reportedly bought about 65% of the team from Walter, but will now own about 83% of the Lakers — and Jeanie Buss apparently will no longer be able to serve as their governor.</p><p>She had been allowed to keep the role at least through 2030 under the deal with Walter, and Iger said last week that the new group planned to honor that arrangement — but governors are required to control at least 15% of team ownership.</p><p>Jerry Buss was a chemist and real estate investor who bought the Lakers, the NHL's Los Angeles Kings and the Forum arena from Jack Kent Cooke in 1979 for $67.5 million. The Lakers quickly entered a renaissance in which they became known for their flashy "Showtime" style of play while winning five NBA titles between 1980 and 1988 behind Magic Johnson and Kareem Abdul-Jabbar.</p><p>While the NBA and professional sports became increasingly more corporate, the Lakers remained essentially a family business despite their massive profile and steady success. Jerry Buss and the Lakers have employed many of the basketball world's greatest players and coaches of the past five decades, and Kobe Bryant led the Lakers to five additional championships between 2000 and 2010 before LeBron James added the 17th in 2020.</p><p>The sale agreement still must be approved by the NBA's board of governors, and the process could take months.</p>

entries.title: Kam McGee, recently named the top junior prospect in the country, leads No. 2 Brother Rice's title defense
entries.summary: <p>It didn’t require the trained eye of a football coach or a prospect analyst to appreciate Brother Rice edge rusher Kameron McGee’s defensive dominance last season.</p><p>McGee led the Crusaders to the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2025/12/03/brother-rice-football-chicago-state-championship-ihsa-st-rita" target="_blank" >Class 7A state title</a> as a sophomore, finishing with 54 tackles, 21 tackles for loss and 10½ sacks. He was a force in the championship-game shutout of rival St. Rita with six tackles, four tackles for loss and two sacks.</p><p>McGee (6-4, 240 pounds) still has two years of high school football to play and is already one of the most impactful defensive players in state history.</p><p>During the summer, 247Sports.com named McGee the No. 1 prospect in the country in the junior class. He’s a top-25 prospect by the overall consensus, but he already has scholarship offers from 44 colleges, including Notre Dame, Alabama, Georgia and most of the Big Ten schools.</p><p>‘‘Whenever anyone asked a question about Kam last year, I said he was the best player in the country,’’ Brother Rice coach Casey Quedenfeld said. ‘‘That hasn’t changed. He does a tremendous job. He’s a really good teammate and has taken an active role in leading guys now. When you are a sophomore, you are kind of figuring things out.’’</p><p>The Crusaders’ starting defense allowed only 5.7 points per game last season, but Notre Dame recruit Brayden Parks (6-3, 305) is the only other starter returning.</p><p>‘‘There are a bunch of young guys that are going to have to step up,’’ McGee said. ‘‘But we are really good where we are. with so few returning starters. Wide receiver Lucas Strang and lineman Ethan Posey (6-4, 290) are the only full-time starters back on offense.</p><p>But there is Power Four talent all over the field. Safety Jonathan Harris has committed to Iowa. Running back Jameson Davis is an Army recruit. Tight end Jack McNamara has scholarship offers from Notre Dame, Ohio State and more. Sophomore offensive lineman CJ Anderson (6-7, 320) is a blossoming prospect.</p><p></p><p>The Crusaders’ offensive line is the largest in school history. Quedenfeld still is figuring out the right starting mix, but there are multiple options, including three transfers from DePaul Prep: brothers Carlos and Lucas Rios and Daniel DeSouza.</p><p></p><p>The plan heading into the season is to play two quarterbacks: senior Rocco Galasso and freshman Sam Holcomb, who already has a scholarship offer from Michigan.</p><p></p><p>‘‘We’ve seen great things from both quarterbacks,’’ Davis said. ‘‘Rocco has been with me since I was a freshman, so I have known what he can do. Sam is just a great all-around talent. He’s a smart kid. When we are in the film room, he is breaking things down as quickly as I am. He has notes on the first game already, every player. It is fun to see him take on something as such a young player. Not many kids can do that as a freshman.’’</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-hangRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-500000" name="module-500000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b>Brother Rice schedule</b><br><ul id="rte-b3bfe312-9a7e-11f1-b687-3f21ac46b653"><li><b>Aug. 21</b> at Lincoln-Way East</li><li><b>Aug. 28</b> vs. Woodlawn</li><li><b>Sept. 4</b> vs. St. Francis</li><li><b>Sept. 11</b> at Loyola</li><li><b>Sept. 18</b> at Notre Dame</li><li><b>Sept. 25</b> vs. Mount Carmel</li><li><b>Oct. 2</b> vs. Fenwick</li><li><b>Oct. 9</b> at DePaul Prep</li><li><b>Oct. 16</b> vs. Marist</li></ul></div> </div><p>Quedenfeld won a state title in his fifth year at Brother Rice. It was a titanic accomplishment for a school that historically had played third fiddle to Mount Carmel and St. Rita in its own backyard. And Marist had been surging for years, as well.</p><p>‘‘When I came here, they told me Brother Rice was a powerhouse,’’ Quedenfeld said. ‘‘I looked at the record books, and Brother Rice was not a powerhouse. We happened to have a really good team last year, and we hope we are on the way this year.
